title: Proposing one-sided tetrons as topological qubits for Majorana-based quantum computation
summary: One-dimensional SM-SC hybrid nanowires with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and applied Zeeman field can support Majorana zero modes (MZMs) at the ends of the wire. In finite-length systems, residual wave-function overlap between the end modes produces an energy splitting. In a two-sided tetron qubit, composed of a pair of parallel Majorana wires coupled by a trivial SC backbone in the middle, this splitting limits the parity lifetime associated with Majorana pairs involving both wires and the coherence of the qubit, adversely affecting measurement-based braiding and readout operations. Here, we propose a one-sided tetron made of four parallel Majorana wires connected at a common end by an SC backbone. In the topological phase, the free wire ends host four MZMs that define the topological qubit, while the Majoranas localized near the opposite ends hybridize through the backbone and acquire finite energy. To study the basic hybridization mechanism, we consider a simpler two-wire subsystem, i.e., half of a one-sided tetron, which we call a doublon. In a doublon, the backbone, or bridge, strongly hybridizes the two Majorana modes at the connected end and shifts them away from zero energy, while the modes at the free ends form a near-zero energy fermion. We show that the splitting of the surviving MZM pair can fall by about two orders of magnitude compared to the splitting energies in a two-sided tetron, thereby dramatically increasing the parity lifetimes. Thus, the one-sided tetron ensures a suppression of the Majorana overlap comparable to doubling the length of the corresponding two-sided tetron.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a one-sided tetron architecture built from four parallel Majorana nanowires joined at a common end by a superconducting backbone, showing that Majorana overlap splitting drops by ~two orders of magnitude versus a two-sided tetron.
AI.motivation: In finite-length SM-SC hybrid nanowires, residual wavefunction overlap between the end Majorana modes causes energy splitting. In a two-sided tetron (a pair of parallel Majorana wires coupled by a trivial SC backbone in the middle), this splitting limits the parity lifetime of Majorana pairs spanning both wires and degrades qubit coherence, harming measurement-based braiding and readout.
AI.method: Propose a one-sided tetron: four parallel Majorana wires connected at a common end by an SC backbone. In the topological phase, the four free wire ends host MZMs defining the qubit, while the opposite-end Majoranas hybridize through the backbone and acquire finite energy. A simpler two-wire subsystem, the doublon (half of a one-sided tetron), is analyzed to study the hybridization mechanism: the bridge strongly hybridizes the two connected-end Majorana modes, shifting them off zero energy, while the free-end modes form a near-zero-energy fermion.
AI.result: The splitting of the surviving MZM pair in the one-sided tetron is reduced by about two orders of magnitude relative to the splitting energies in a two-sided tetron, dramatically increasing parity lifetimes.
AI.conclusion: The one-sided tetron suppresses Majorana overlap comparably to doubling the length of the corresponding two-sided tetron, offering a geometry that improves parity lifetime and qubit coherence without requiring longer wires.

title: Composite Fermion Theory of Fractional Chern Insulators in Rhombohedral Graphene
summary: The experimental observation of the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect in rhombohedral graphene multilayers has raised questions about the nature of the fractional Chern insulator (FCI) states and the role of the moiré potential. In this Letter we develop a composite fermion (CF) description and discuss how moiré modulation and Coulomb interactions stabilize the FCI ground states. Under a flux-attachment transformation and mean-field approximation, the CF spectrum forms Landau levels that are further split by the moiré potential. At moiré filling fractions in the Jain sequence, an integer number of CF bands are occupied, resulting in an incompressible ground state with fractionally quantized Hall response. Remarkably, when the attached flux opposes the Berry curvature of the conduction band of rhombohedral graphene, the CF Landau levels are widely spaced in energy and delocalized across layers, leading to a reduced density of states that helps protect the CF mean-field state and amplifying effects of the moiré potential acting on the layer away from the doped electrons. Interactions between CFs further enlarge the moiré-induced band gap and stabilize the FCI ground state. Our work sheds light on the nature of the FCI states in rhombohedral graphene and provides a new theoretical framework for further studies.

AI.tldr: This Letter develops a composite fermion (CF) description to explain how moiré modulation and Coulomb interactions stabilize fractional Chern insulator (FCI) ground states in rhombohedral graphene multilayers, where the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect has been observed.
AI.motivation: The experimental observation of the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect in rhombohedral graphene multilayers has raised open questions about the nature of the FCI states and the specific role played by the moiré potential. A theoretical framework was needed to clarify how these states form and are stabilized.
AI.method: The authors apply a flux-attachment transformation followed by a mean-field approximation to construct a composite fermion description. In this picture, the CF spectrum forms Landau levels that are further split by the moiré potential. They analyze the system at moiré filling fractions in the Jain sequence, where an integer number of CF bands are occupied. They also examine the case where the attached flux opposes the Berry curvature of the conduction band of rhombohedral graphene, and study the effect of CF-CF interactions.

When the attached flux opposes the conduction-band Berry curvature, the CF Landau levels are widely spaced in energy and delocalized across layers, reducing the density of states, which helps protect the CF mean-field state and amplifies the effects of the moiré potential acting on the layer away from the doped electrons. Interactions between CFs further enlarge the moiré-induced band gap and stabilize the FCI ground state.
AI.conclusion: The work sheds light on the nature of the FCI states in rhombohedral graphene and provides a new theoretical framework for further studies.

title: Adjoint-State Identifiability of Piezo-Tunable Valley Splitting in 2D Magnetic Heterostructures
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables (including Supplementary Material). Custom adjoint-state codes and simulation dataset are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22850138
summary: Controlling valley degrees of freedom with mechanical strain is a promising approach for solid-state information processing. Current theoretical literature routinely predicts strain-tuned valley splitting at the microscopic level but rarely evaluates whether these quantum predictions remain statistically recoverable in realistic macroscopic devices. This manuscript establishes a fully classical, partial differential equation-constrained multiscale inverse framework for quantifying the device-level identifiability of predicted strain-tunable valley effects in two-dimensional magnetic heterostructures, demonstrated here for a molybdenum disulfide and chromium tribromide heterostructure. First-principles structural relaxations confirm a chiral $C_3$ point-group symmetry which mathematically reduces the relevant exchange-strain coupling tensor to a single scalar. A partial differential equation-constrained adjoint-state architecture successfully bridges continuum elastodynamics to valley-resolved anomalous Hall transport. Density functional theory yields a coupling estimate of $η\approx -0.07$ meV whose 95% confidence interval is consistent with zero. Evaluating this specific coupling magnitude against established thermal noise and velocity saturation limits defines a safe operating window bounded between 262.0 and 22,337.6 V/cm. Rather than asserting a confirmed nonzero material property this bounded operational window functions as a precise diagnostic threshold. Deploying this rigorous statistical identifiability framework provides a necessary mathematical filter to determine the true experimental viability of theoretically predicted two-dimensional materials before complex physical fabrication.

AI.motivation: Theoretical literature routinely predicts microscopic strain-tuned valley splitting, yet rarely evaluates whether these quantum predictions remain statistically recoverable in realistic macroscopic devices. A mathematical filter is needed to determine experimental viability before costly fabrication.

title: Contact-Governed Macroscopic Signatures of Strain-Induced Valley Sorting in MoS$_2$ Field-Effect Transistors
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Custom SILVACO TCAD scripts, COMSOL files and datasets are all available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21346193
summary: Strain engineering is a leading route to control valley-selective transport in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides. Whether this quantum effect survives inside a fully contacted device remains an open question. Quantum transport models capture the underlying valley deflection but are limited to isolated nanoscale fragments, leaving it unclear if a full device registers strain-induced valley sorting in the bulk, at the contacts, or at all. Here, the quantum valley-deflection tensor of strained monolayer MoS$_2$ is embedded directly into a macroscopic Poisson-drift-diffusion model, extending this physics to a complete, contact-inclusive device. Applying this framework to a 300~nm monolayer MoS$_2$ transistor with a 3~nm HfO$_2$ gate dielectric at 77~K, under a localized 6.14~T pseudo-magnetic strain field, shows the resulting 63.6\% suppression of the ON-state current is not a bulk property. It is set almost entirely by the source and drain metal-semiconductor interfaces. The full suppression is reproduced when only the 15~nm contact regions are strained and nearly vanishes when the channel interior alone is strained, identifying the metal contact as the dominant site of strain-induced valley physics. Observing it requires tunneling-transparent, degenerately-doped contacts, since classical Ohmic barriers overwhelm the topological signal. A transmission-line analysis reduces this behavior to a single valley-topological contact resistance ($R_{c,V}$) and a predictive inverse-length scaling law. This framework applies to any strain-engineered 2D-material heterostructure and can be tested with standard multi-length contact structures. Ultimately, these results identify the metal-semiconductor interface as the decisive location for engineering and detecting valley-selective transport in real 2D-material devices.

title: Correlated Low-Energy Model of Monolayer 1H-NbS$_2$: A cRPA+DMFT Study
summary: Monolayer $1\mathrm{H}\text{-}\mathrm{NbS}_2$ hosts a well-separated metallic band of predominant Nb-$d_{z^2}$ character, providing an ideal platform to probe electronic correlations within a single-band setting. In this work, we present a comprehensive study of $1\mathrm{H}\text{-}\mathrm{NbS}_2$ by combining first-principles Wannier interpolation, constrained random-phase approximation (cRPA), and DFT+DMFT. We show that an effective single-band model accurately captures the low-energy electronic structure, reproducing key experimental features from ARPES and STS $dI/dV$ spectra, including a characteristic Van Hove singularity. While static DFT+$U$ fails to describe the correlated metallic nature of the system, DFT+DMFT successfully accounts for the spectral weight redistribution and dynamic correlations. By defining the cRPA target subspace directly within the isolated Nb-$d_{z^2}$ band, we obtain a renormalized local interaction of $U_{\mathrm{cRPA}} = 1.138~\mathrm{eV}$. This interaction stabilizes a strongly correlated metallic state that remains robust upon cooling. Remarkably, this minimal single-band model captures a spectral broadening similar to that previously reported in more elaborate treatments - incorporating larger local interactions ($U \sim 1.8~\mathrm{eV}$, derived from a multiorbital cRPA construction), intersite Coulomb terms ($V$), and electron-phonon coupling - demonstrating that a consistently downfolded local interaction alone can already capture key aspects of the experimentally observed low-energy behavior of monolayer $1\mathrm{H}\text{-}\mathrm{NbS}_2$.

AI.tldr: A combined Wannier/cRPA/DFT+DMFT study shows that an effective single-band model with a downfolded local interaction U_cRPA = 1.138 eV captures the correlated metallic state and low-energy spectral features of monolayer 1H-NbS2, reproducing ARPES and STS dI/dV data including the Van Hove singularity.
AI.motivation: Monolayer 1H-NbS2 features a well-separated metallic band of predominant Nb-d_z2 character, making it an ideal single-band platform to probe electronic correlations. The goal is to determine whether a minimal single-band description with a consistently downfolded interaction suffices to reproduce experimentally observed low-energy behavior.
AI.method: First-principles Wannier interpolation for an effective single-band model, constrained random-phase approximation (cRPA) with the target subspace defined directly within the isolated Nb-d_z2 band, and DFT+DMFT calculations; comparison with static DFT+U and with more elaborate prior treatments (multiorbital cRPA U ~ 1.8 eV, intersite Coulomb V, electron-phonon coupling); validation against ARPES and STS dI/dV spectra.
AI.result: The effective single-band model reproduces key experimental features including a characteristic Van Hove singularity. Static DFT+U fails to describe the correlated metallic nature, whereas DFT+DMFT captures spectral weight redistribution and dynamic correlations. The cRPA downfolding yields a renormalized local interaction U_cRPA = 1.138 eV, which stabilizes a strongly correlated metallic state robust upon cooling. This minimal model reproduces spectral broadening comparable to that of more elaborate treatments.
AI.conclusion: A consistently downfolded local interaction alone within a minimal single-band model can capture key aspects of the experimentally observed low-energy behavior of monolayer 1H-NbS2, establishing single-band DFT+DMFT with cRPA-derived U as a sufficient and efficient description of its correlated metallic state.

title: A density-based topology optimization framework for steady Navier-Stokes flow with design-dependent wall actuation
summary: Design-dependent wall velocities are difficult to treat in density-based fluid topology optimization. This difficulty arises because the fluid-solid interface is represented implicitly and evolves with the design. This paper proposes a diffuse-interface formulation for topology optimization of steady incompressible Navier-Stokes flows with design-dependent wall actuation. A continuous topological description field parameterized by compactly supported radial basis functions (CS-RBFs) provides the local interface orientation, and its regularized projection defines the pseudo-density for Brinkman flow analysis. The wall velocity is imposed on a fixed mesh through an equivalent volumetric momentum source, which is localized by a diffuse-interface measure constructed from the pseudo-density and the gradient of the description field. Assuming a locally planar interface and uniformly distributed Wendland radial basis functions, the source coefficient is determined analytically by balancing the equivalent momentum input with the Brinkman resistance at the interface center. These assumptions also yield a characteristic transition-width estimate in terms of the projection steepness and support radius. Continuous adjoint analysis is performed to derive the design sensitivities. Two- and three-dimensional examples formulated using the analogy equation demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed topology optimization method for flow-rate maximization. Body-fitted re-simulations verify the flow fields and transport performance of the optimized designs. The formulation is further extended to electroosmotic transport under the thin electric double layer (EDL) assumption using the Helmholtz-Smoluchowski relation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a diffuse-interface formulation for density-based topology optimization of steady incompressible Navier-Stokes flows with design-dependent wall velocities, using compactly supported RBFs and an equivalent volumetric momentum source.
AI.motivation: Design-dependent wall velocities are difficult to handle in density-based fluid topology optimization because the fluid-solid interface is implicit and evolves with the design, complicating the imposition of boundary actuation.
AI.method: A continuous topological description field parameterized by compactly supported radial basis functions (CS-RBFs) provides local interface orientation; its regularized projection defines pseudo-density for Brinkman flow analysis. Wall velocity is imposed via an equivalent volumetric momentum source localized by a diffuse-interface measure built from pseudo-density and description-field gradient. Assuming a locally planar interface and uniformly distributed Wendland RBFs, the source coefficient is derived analytically by balancing momentum input with Brinkman resistance at the interface center, yielding a transition-width estimate. Continuous adjoint analysis derives design sensitivities.
AI.result: Two- and three-dimensional flow-rate maximization examples demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Body-fitted re-simulations verify flow fields and transport performance of optimized designs. The formulation extends to electroosmotic transport under the thin EDL assumption via the Helmholtz-Smoluchowski relation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diffuse-interface formulation enables effective topology optimization of flows with design-dependent wall actuation, validated numerically and extendable to electroosmotic transport.

title: Time-Reversal Selection Rule for Twist Disorder
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, plus 61 pages of Supplemental Material with 19 figures
summary: Random layer rotations are ubiquitous in layered matter, from turbostratic films to rotationally disordered crystals, and strongly suppress transport across the layers. Generated by a symmetry operation, this disorder is absent on the rotation axis, so the thickness laws of conduction are set by how fast backscattering vanishes there. We show that a time-reversal selection rule decides this: each twist harmonic of the interlayer bond is either a frame rotation, whose backscattering cancels, or a coupling change, which scatters. A zero-set theorem turns the rule into universal thickness laws for electrons and phonons, fixed by band-edge symmetry; random twist increments rescale the backscattering but keep its order. Where the axis is unprotected, band nodes provide a second route: a transparent energy with heavy-tailed disorder and an $N^{-3}$ law. A first-principles forward-channel model of black phosphorus shows both routes; its random-twist films act as a symmetry filter that, relative to aligned stacks, retains a hundred times more of the electron than of the hole conductance at 64 layers. The symmetry of band edges and phonon branches thus decides what crosses a disordered stack, making stacking disorder a design element.

AI.tldr: Random interlayer rotations in layered matter suppress cross-layer transport, and the resulting thickness scaling laws are governed by a time-reversal selection rule that classifies twist harmonics into non-scattering frame rotations versus scattering coupling changes.
AI.motivation: Random layer rotations (turbostratic films, rotationally disordered crystals) strongly suppress interlayer transport. Because this disorder vanishes on the rotation axis, the thickness laws of conduction depend on how quickly backscattering disappears there—motivating a symmetry-based framework to predict transport scaling.
AI.method: The authors establish a time-reversal selection rule: each twist harmonic of the interlayer bond is either a frame rotation (backscattering cancels) or a coupling change (scatters). A zero-set theorem converts this rule into universal thickness laws for electrons and phonons fixed by band-edge symmetry, with random twist increments rescaling backscattering while preserving its order. A first-principles forward-channel model of black phosphorus is used to demonstrate the mechanism.
AI.result: Two routes for conduction are identified: symmetry-protected axis conduction following universal thickness laws, and, in unprotected cases, band nodes yielding a transparent energy with heavy-tailed disorder and an N^-3 law. In black phosphorus, random-twist films act as a symmetry filter, retaining ~100× more electron than hole conductance at 64 layers relative to aligned stacks.
AI.conclusion: Band-edge and phonon-branch symmetry determines which carriers cross a disordered stack. Stacking disorder therefore becomes a design element, enabling symmetry-selective transport control in layered materials.

title: Luttinger Liquid Behavior in a Single-Layer Nickelate La1.4Sr0.6NiO4
summary: The discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in bilayer and trilayer nickelates has spurred intense interest in the Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates; yet the fundamental properties of the NiO2 layer remain obscured by interlayer coupling. It is therefore imperative to investigate the electronic properties of their single-layer counterpart to isolate the intrinsic physics of the NiO layer. In this work, we present a systematic study of the single-layer nickelate La1.4Sr0.6NiO4 using high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and theoretical calculations. We reveal strong electron correlation effects, manifested by high-energy kinks in band dispersions and a pronounced orbital-dependent band renormalization. Interestingly, we observe a quasi-one-dimensional electronic structure characterized by straight Fermi surface sheets along the diagonal momentum directions. Such square Fermi surface topology facilitates non-Fermi liquid behavior consistent with the Luttinger liquid model, as evidenced by the power-law spectral function, robust temperature scaling, and the observation of spin-charge separation. Our results therefore not only unveil an exotic Luttinger liquid behavior emerging from the unexpected dimensional reduction in an intrinsically quasi-two-dimensional nickelate but also provide a new perspective for understanding the intriguing physics in multilayer nickelates.

AI.tldr: Systematic ARPES and theoretical study of single-layer nickelate La1.4Sr0.6NiO4 reveals strong electron correlations and a quasi-one-dimensional electronic structure with square Fermi surface topology, giving rise to non-Fermi liquid (Luttinger liquid) behavior via dimensional reduction in an intrinsically quasi-two-dimensional material.
AI.motivation: High-temperature superconductivity in bilayer and trilayer nickelates has drawn intense interest in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates, but the intrinsic properties of the NiO2 layer are obscured by interlayer coupling. Investigating the single-layer counterpart is therefore imperative to isolate the intrinsic physics of the NiO layer.
AI.method: High-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) combined with theoretical calculations on single-layer nickelate La1.4Sr0.6NiO4.
AI.result: Strong electron correlation effects are revealed, manifested by high-energy kinks in band dispersions and pronounced orbital-dependent band renormalization. A quasi-one-dimensional electronic structure with straight Fermi surface sheets along diagonal momentum directions is observed. This square Fermi surface topology supports non-Fermi liquid behavior consistent with the Luttinger liquid model, evidenced by a power-law spectral function, robust temperature scaling, and spin-charge separation.
AI.conclusion: The results unveil exotic Luttinger liquid behavior emerging from unexpected dimensional reduction in an intrinsically quasi-two-dimensional nickelate, and provide a new perspective for understanding the intriguing physics of multilayer nickelates.

title: Asymptotic Analysis of Empirical Risk Minimization on Entry-wise i.i.d. Heavy-Tailed Data
summary: Many real-world datasets exhibit unusually large values far more frequently than predicted by Gaussian models. Heavy-tailed distributions capture this behavior, yet evaluating learning performance under them remains challenging because rare, large feature entries retain non-vanishing effects even in high dimensions. Even in the canonical setting of empirical risk minimization for linear regression with entry-wise i.i.d. symmetric $α$-stable data, a precise asymptotic characterization of prediction has been lacking. In this work, we introduce a functional order parameter that describes the random effective problem associated with each coefficient. Using the replica method, we fully characterize the generalization error in the proportional high-dimensional limit where the sample size and feature dimension diverge at a fixed ratio. Additionally, this analysis establishes a heavy-tail universality law, scaling laws relating typical errors to prediction reliability, and the Bayes-optimal prediction error. In addition to characterizing the effects of extreme entries on the learning process, our method applies broadly to other systems with persistent local heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a precise asymptotic characterization of generalization error for empirical risk minimization in linear regression under entry-wise i.i.d. symmetric α-stable (heavy-tailed) data, using a functional order parameter and the replica method in the proportional high-dimensional limit.
AI.motivation: Real-world datasets frequently exhibit large values far more often than Gaussian models predict, and heavy-tailed distributions capture this. However, evaluating learning performance under heavy tails is difficult because rare, large feature entries retain non-vanishing effects even in high dimensions. Even for canonical linear regression with entry-wise i.i.d. symmetric α-stable data, a precise asymptotic characterization of prediction had been lacking.
AI.method: The authors introduce a functional order parameter that describes the random effective problem associated with each coefficient. Using the replica method, they analyze the proportional high-dimensional limit where sample size and feature dimension diverge at a fixed ratio.
AI.result: The analysis fully characterizes the generalization error in the proportional high-dimensional limit. It additionally establishes a heavy-tail universality law, scaling laws relating typical errors to prediction reliability, and the Bayes-optimal prediction error. It also characterizes the effects of extreme entries on the learning process.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a precise asymptotic theory of learning under heavy-tailed data for linear regression, yielding universality and scaling laws, and the method applies broadly to other systems exhibiting persistent local heterogeneity.

title: Data geometry preserves prediction but reshapes explanation
summary: Across scientific domains, empirical data often give rise to positive semidefinite matrices that encode similarities, couplings or interactions and induce natural geometries. We investigate whether changing the geometry used to compare the same empirical representations preserves subject-level performance and the local structures from which explanations are derived, a question we term the prediction explanation invariance problem. We address this problem across morphometric MRI, fMRI and EEG data by comparing Frobenius and trace geometries applied to the same empirical matrices. Predictive performance was broadly preserved across geometries, but comparable performance did not imply agreement in subject-level decision scores or predicted labels. Predictive similarity also masked geometry-dependent differences in local neighbourhoods, perturbation sensitivities and explanatory rankings. Dimensionality reduction made the two subject-space geometries progressively more concordant, while classification performance and decision-level agreement declined. These results identify data geometry as a hidden degree of freedom in explainability: similar performance does not guarantee invariant decisions or explanations.

AI.tldr: Comparing Frobenius and trace geometries on the same positive semidefinite matrices (morphometric MRI, fMRI, EEG) shows that preserved predictive performance does not guarantee invariant subject-level decisions or explanations, identifying data geometry as a hidden degree of freedom in explainability.
AI.motivation: Empirical data across scientific domains yield positive semidefinite matrices encoding similarities, couplings, or interactions that induce natural geometries. It is unclear whether changing the geometry used to compare the same empirical representations preserves subject-level performance and the local structures underlying explanations—a question framed as the prediction explanation invariance problem.
AI.method: Across morphometric MRI, fMRI, and EEG datasets, Frobenius and trace geometries were applied to the same empirical matrices. The study compared predictive performance, subject-level decision scores and predicted labels, local neighbourhoods, perturbation sensitivities, explanatory rankings, and the effect of dimensionality reduction on geometry concordance.
AI.result: Predictive performance was broadly preserved across geometries, but comparable performance did not imply agreement in subject-level decision scores or predicted labels. Predictive similarity masked geometry-dependent differences in local neighbourhoods, perturbation sensitivities, and explanatory rankings. Dimensionality reduction made the two subject-space geometries progressively more concordant, while classification performance and decision-level agreement declined.
AI.conclusion: Data geometry is a hidden degree of freedom in explainability: similar performance does not guarantee invariant decisions or explanations. Geometry choice must be treated as a substantive analytical decision rather than a neutral one.

title: Towards Accurate MHz Core Loss Measurements
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Miniaturized magnetic components play an important role in achieving high efficiency and high power density in power converters. Accurate core loss data are essential when optimizing magnetic components, but making accurate core loss measurements remains challenging, especially at MHz frequencies. As a result, many research groups have developed their own testers in pursuit of improved accuracy, and the amount of published core loss data has increased. However, large variations in these data shed light on fundamental barriers to accurate MHz core loss measurement. This paper identifies these barriers and presents methods for overcoming them.

AI.tldr: Accurate MHz core loss measurement is hindered by fundamental barriers, and this paper identifies them and proposes methods to overcome them.
AI.motivation: Miniaturized magnetic components are key to high-efficiency, high-power-density power converters, and optimizing them requires accurate core loss data. However, accurate core loss measurement remains challenging, particularly at MHz frequencies.
AI.method: The paper identifies the fundamental barriers to accurate MHz core loss measurement and presents methods for overcoming them.
AI.result: Although many research groups have built their own testers and published more core loss data, large variations in these data reveal fundamental barriers to accurate MHz core loss measurement.
AI.conclusion: Identifying and overcoming these barriers is essential for obtaining accurate MHz core loss data needed to optimize miniaturized magnetic components.

title: Kaonic Atom X-ray Spectroscopy: From SIDDHARTA-2 to the EXKALIBUR Program
summary: X-ray spectroscopy of kaonic atoms offers a unique experimental window on the interplay between low-energy strong interaction and precision atomic physics studies. This article reviews the scientific progress achieved with SIDDHARTA-2 at DAFNE and discusses how it shapes the next generation measurements. Particular emphasis is given to EXKALIBUR, a multifacility program designed to perform measurements of kaon-nucleus interactions across the periodic table and to extend kaonic atom spectroscopy toward precision tests of bound-state QED and the charged-kaon mass extraction. The first proposed strong interaction campaign at J-PARC aims to investigate kaonic atoms with solid Li, Be, and B targets using new 1-mm-thick Silicon Drift Detectors and high-resolution TES microcalorimeters, exploiting isotope pairs to isolate nuclear-structure and kaon-multinucleon effects. Measurements of Mg, Al, Si, and S with CdZnTe detectors will broaden this study toward heavier nuclei. EXKALIBUR will establish a systematic experimental framework for testing low-energy strong interaction with strangeness and bound-state QED predictions across a broad range of kaonic atoms.

AI.tldr: This review summarizes SIDDHARTA-2's kaonic atom results at DAFNE and introduces EXKALIBUR, a multifacility program to probe kaon-nucleus interactions across the periodic table, including a J-PARC campaign on Li, Be, B, Mg, Al, Si, and S to test low-energy strong interaction and bound-state QED.
AI.motivation: Kaonic atom X-ray spectroscopy provides a unique probe of low-energy strong interaction and atomic physics. SIDDHARTA-2's achievements motivate a broader, systematic program—EXKALIBUR—to test strangeness-driven strong interaction and bound-state QED, and to extract the charged-kaon mass with higher precision.
AI.method: The review examines SIDDHARTA-2 progress at DAFNE and describes EXKALIBUR's proposed measurements: (1) a J-PARC strong interaction campaign using solid Li, Be, and B targets with 1-mm-thick Silicon Drift Detectors and high-resolution TES microcalorimeters, exploiting isotope pairs to isolate nuclear-structure and kaon-multinucleon effects; (2) Mg, Al, Si, and S measurements with CdZnTe detectors to extend the study to heavier nuclei.
AI.result: EXKALIBUR is designed to deliver precision measurements of kaon-nucleus interactions across the periodic table, providing data for tests of bound-state QED and charged-kaon mass extraction.
AI.conclusion: EXKALIBUR will establish a systematic experimental framework for testing low-energy strong interaction with strangeness and bound-state QED predictions across a broad range of kaonic atoms.

title: A numerical and efficient model for thermo-field electron emission calculations
summary: As electron sources are reduced in size, fabricated in new materials, or pushed for performance, the analytical formulations for thermo-field electron emission, namely Fowler-Nordheim and Murphy-Good equations and their JWKB-based extensions, are increasingly applied out of the range of conditions for which they were derived. We present GETELEC-3, an open-source code that replaces them with a direct numerical solution of the one-dimensional time-independent Schrödinger equation (1D-TISE). Several methods to solve the 1D-TISE have been implemented to test for speed, robustness, and solution's uncertainty. The Noumerov algorithm is found to be quickest, with the solution uncertainty below 1%, and together with an optimised kernel that advances all electron energies in parallel, the cost of calculating the current density is reduced to a few milliseconds - comparable to the JWKB evaluation. To further boost the calculation speed, especially in complicated barriers, a neural network has been trained on the residual of the logarithm of the semiclassical reference and it reproduces the current density better than 0.4% at a fraction of the computational cost. The code is developed for metals and semiconductors, accepts arbitrary potentials and density of states, and comes with a user-friendly interface and compiled executable to democratise rigorous electron emission calculations and data analysis.

AI.tldr: GETELEC-3 is an open-source code that replaces analytical thermo-field electron emission formulations with a direct numerical solution of the 1D time-independent Schrödinger equation, using the fast Noumerov algorithm and a neural-network accelerator to compute current density within milliseconds at sub-1% and sub-0.4% uncertainty.
AI.motivation: As electron sources shrink, adopt new materials, or are driven for higher performance, analytical formulations such as Fowler-Nordheim and Murphy-Good equations and their JWKB-based extensions are increasingly applied outside the conditions for which they were derived, undermining their accuracy.
AI.method: GETELEC-3 directly solves the one-dimensional time-independent Schrödinger equation (1D-TISE). Several solution methods are benchmarked for speed, robustness, and uncertainty; the Noumerov algorithm is selected and paired with an optimised parallel kernel advancing all electron energies simultaneously. A neural network is trained on the residual of the logarithm of the semiclassical reference to accelerate calculations in complicated barriers.
AI.result: Noumerov is the fastest method with solution uncertainty below 1%; with the parallel kernel, current-density evaluation drops to a few milliseconds, comparable to JWKB evaluation. The neural network reproduces current density better than 0.4% at a fraction of the computational cost.
AI.conclusion: GETELEC-3 supports metals and semiconductors, accepts arbitrary potentials and density of states, and provides a user-friendly interface and compiled executable, democratising rigorous electron emission calculations and data analysis.

title: Is there a density-gradient expansion for the electronic exchange energy?
summary: An old but recurring question in ground-state density functional theory, relevant to the construction of density functional approximations, is the existence of a second-order gradient expansion for the exchange energy that is exact for densities that vary slowly over space. Here we will argue that there is such an expansion, with a gradient coefficient 10/7 of Sham's, as suggested by theoretical/mathematical derivations and by numerical calculations on model slowly-varying metallic densities, although some standard derivations do not quite capture the correct gradient coefficient. We also discuss long-range anomalies in the gradient expansions for the exchange and correlation holes around an electron. It is plausible that, as suggested earlier and recently, standard derivations are still correct for the coefficient of the second-order gradient expansion for exchange and correlation together, in which case the correct gradient coefficient for correlation is $C_{\mathrm{c}}$ = $C_{\mathrm{xc}}$ - $C_{\mathrm{x}}$. We propose possible numerical evaluations of $C_{\mathrm{xc}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{x}}$ that are free from long-range anomalies, and discuss implications for density functional approximations. Axel Becke's 1988 generalized gradient approximation (the B88 GGA) for the exchange energy brought density functional theory into chemistry, with a gradient coefficient for exchange that is optimal at the GGA level for atoms and molecules but too large for solids. Meta-GGAs seem to work as well for molecules as for solids, but may not be perfected yet. The article concludes with a few memories that the first author has of discussions with Axel Becke.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that a second-order gradient expansion for exchange energy exists with a gradient coefficient of 10/7 of Sham's, supported by theoretical and numerical evidence on slowly-varying metallic densities, and discusses long-range anomalies, correlation coefficients, and implications for density functional approximations including Becke's B88 GGA.
AI.motivation: A recurring question in ground-state density functional theory concerns whether a second-order gradient expansion for exchange energy exists that is exact for slowly varying densities. This matters for constructing density functional approximations. Standard derivations may not capture the correct gradient coefficient, motivating clarification of the correct expansion and its coefficient.
AI.method: The authors present theoretical/mathematical derivations and numerical calculations on model slowly-varying metallic densities. They analyze long-range anomalies in gradient expansions for exchange and correlation holes, and propose numerical evaluations of C_xc and C_x free from long-range anomalies.
AI.result: There exists a second-order gradient expansion with gradient coefficient 10/7 of Sham's, consistent with theory and numerical tests. Standard derivations may still be correct for the combined exchange-correlation coefficient, implying C_c = C_xc - C_x. Becke's B88 GGA uses a gradient coefficient optimal for atoms/molecules but too large for solids; meta-GGAs perform comparably for molecules and solids but may not be perfected.
AI.conclusion: The correct exchange gradient coefficient is 10/7 of Sham's, with implications for density functional approximations. Proposed anomaly-free numerical evaluations of C_xc and C_x can guide future approximations. The article closes with the first author's memories of discussions with Axel Becke.

title: Theory of resonance Raman profiles in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers: Interference effects due to inter-valley phonon scattering
summary: The optical properties of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) are strongly impacted by exciton-phonon coupling, especially inter-valley scattering in the case of tungsten-based materials. Together with strain-tunability of the energetic K-Q valley separation this material class therefore provides a platform for semiconductor optomechanics. Here we investigate the influence of inter-valley scattering and strain on resonance Raman scattering in monolayer TMDCs using a microscopic model based on an effective deformation potential coupling for the exciton-phonon interaction. Considering exemplarily the resonance Raman profile of the A$_1$-mode in hBN-encapsulated monolayer WSe$_2$, we find that inter-valley scattering between the electronic K- and Q-valley leads to destructive interference between a first order and a third order Raman process. As a result we obtain a suppression of the incoming resonance in WSe$_2$, consistent with recently published experimental data.

AI.tldr: Inter-valley scattering causes destructive interference between first- and third-order Raman processes, suppressing the incoming resonance of the A1-mode in monolayer WSe2, in agreement with experiments.
AI.motivation: The optical properties of monolayer TMDCs are strongly influenced by exciton-phonon coupling, particularly inter-valley scattering in tungsten-based materials. Combined with strain-tunable K-Q valley separation, this offers a platform for semiconductor optomechanics, motivating a microscopic understanding of how inter-valley scattering and strain affect resonance Raman scattering.
AI.method: A microscopic model based on an effective deformation potential coupling for the exciton-phonon interaction is used, applied exemplarily to the resonance Raman profile of the A1-mode in hBN-encapsulated monolayer WSe2.
AI.result: Inter-valley scattering between the electronic K- and Q-valleys induces destructive interference between a first-order and a third-order Raman process, producing a suppression of the incoming resonance in WSe2. This is consistent with recently published experimental data.
AI.conclusion: Inter-valley scattering and strain govern resonance Raman scattering in monolayer TMDCs, and the model reproduces the experimentally observed suppression of the incoming resonance in WSe2.

title: Disorder into Correlation: A Microscopic Mechanism for Sub-McIntyre Avalanche Noise
summary: Avalanche multiplication is intrinsically stochastic, yet experiments reveal excess noise below the minimum predicted by McIntyre's local-field theory. The microscopic origin of this noise suppression remains incompletely understood. We show that polar-optical-phonon emission, confined to a narrow forward cone, competes with elastic alloy scattering that diffuses field-collimated hot carriers out of the cone. Suppressed phonon cooling narrows the ionization path beyond the dead space and synchronizes successive ionizations into a dynamic staircase. This explains the low noise of Sb-based alloys and HgCdTe and makes alloy disorder a design parameter.

AI.tldr: Polar-optical-phonon emission confined to a narrow forward cone competes with elastic alloy scattering that diffuses field-collimated hot carriers out of the cone; suppressed phonon cooling narrows the ionization path and synchronizes successive ionizations into a dynamic staircase, explaining sub-McIntyre excess noise in Sb-based alloys and HgCdTe and establishing alloy disorder as a design parameter.
AI.motivation: Avalanche multiplication is intrinsically stochastic, yet experiments show excess noise below McIntyre's local-field minimum, and the microscopic origin of this noise suppression is incompletely understood.
AI.method: Theoretical microscopic analysis of competing scattering mechanisms: polar-optical-phonon emission restricted to a narrow forward cone vs. elastic alloy scattering that diffuses field-collimated hot carriers out of that cone.
AI.result: Suppressed phonon cooling narrows the ionization path beyond the dead space and synchronizes successive ionizations into a dynamic staircase, accounting for the low excess noise observed in Sb-based alloys and HgCdTe.
AI.conclusion: Phonon-emission/alloy-scattering competition governs noise suppression in avalanche multiplication, and alloy disorder can be treated as a tunable design parameter for low-noise avalanche devices.

title: Constitutive-Set Mechanics: variational mechanics on an admissible set of constitutive laws
summary: A structural simulation needs a constitutive law, and experiments rarely determine one uniquely: several laws may fit the same data and satisfy the same physical constraints, yet differ where the structure is loaded in ways the tests never were. Constitutive-Set Mechanics (CSM) keeps all of those laws. It replaces the single law in the variational formulation by the admissible set, and lets the mechanics itself decide which members of the set affect the structural prediction. The framework rests on one observation: a finite element assembly consults the law only at the strains the structure reaches, so the incremental energy depends on the law through a weighted record of those strains, the occupation measure of the state. The energy of a state under the set is a support function on that measure, and the equilibrium solve one performs anyway supplies the information needed to bound the worst case. Equilibrium states become certificates on the robust response, rigorous on the upper side for any mechanics solver and two-sided under global minimisation; the certificate has at most one more state than the number of constitutive directions the structure interrogates; a coherence theorem identifies when the pointwise-worst material is one no single material can be; and constitutive inference acts on the same support function. The method is demonstrated on linear elasticity, a data-constrained constitutive function, phase-field fracture, an assembled finite-strain composite shell, and a membrane characterised by one-mode tests alone. On the shell the structure interrogates four of 226 constitutive directions; on the membrane the certified worst-case energy exceeds the reference more than fourfold, and the experiment that most contracts the certified prediction is not the one where the constitutive uncertainty is largest.

AI.tldr: Constitutive-Set Mechanics (CSM) replaces the single constitutive law in a variational formulation with the admissible set of laws, letting the mechanics decide which members affect the structural prediction. The incremental energy depends on the law through the occupation measure of reached strains, so the energy of a state is a support function on that measure, and equilibrium solves yield certificates on the robust response.
AI.motivation: A structural simulation requires a constitutive law, but experiments rarely determine one uniquely: multiple laws can fit the same data and satisfy the same physical constraints while diverging in loading regimes the tests never probed. Rather than committing to a single law, one should retain all admissible laws and let the mechanics identify which of them matter for the structural prediction.
AI.method: CSM keeps the entire admissible set of constitutive laws in place of a single law and embeds it in the variational formulation. It exploits the fact that a finite element assembly consults the law only at the strains the structure reaches, making the incremental energy depend on the law through a weighted record of these strains—the occupation measure of the state. The energy of a state under the set becomes a support function on that measure, and the equilibrium solve already performed provides the information needed to bound the worst case. Equilibrium states serve as certificates: rigorous on the upper side for any mechanics solver and two-sided under global minimisation, with at most one more state than the number of interrogated constitutive directions.
AI.result: The framework yields a coherence theorem identifying when the pointwise-worst material cannot be realised by any single material, and it shows constitutive inference acts on the same support function. It is demonstrated on linear elasticity, a data-constrained constitutive function, phase-field fracture, an assembled finite-strain composite shell, and a membrane characterised by one-mode tests alone. On the shell, the structure interrogates only four of 226 constitutive directions; on the membrane, the certified worst-case energy exceeds the reference more than fourfold, and the experiment that most contracts the certified prediction is not the one with the largest constitutive uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: CSM provides a rigorous, solver-agnostic route to robust structural prediction under non-unique constitutive laws by retaining the full admissible set and extracting certificates from standard equilibrium solves. Its certificates are one-sided (upper) in general and two-sided under global minimisation, with cost tied to the number of constitutive directions the structure actually interrogates. The demonstrations highlight two practical insights: structures often interrogate only a small subset of available constitutive directions, and reducing prediction uncertainty is not equivalent to minimising constitutive uncertainty.

title: Interplay between spinodal decomposition and wetting in ternary to quinary mixtures
summary: We use two-dimensional phase-field simulations based on the Cahn--Hilliard description to study spinodal decomposition in N-component mixtures with N = 3, 4, 5. In particular, we consider surface-directed spinodal decomposition in which one of the coexisting phases serves as a filler particle, while the remaining components phase separate around its surface. We investigate both nonwetting and wetting conditions by varying the interfacial tensions between the particle and the other components. The competition between wetting kinetics and spinodal decomposition produces rich morphological evolution, including the formation of lattice, droplet, and target (or core-shell) morphologies. The target pattern consists of alternating component-rich rings around the particle. In the intermediate-to-late time regime, these structures undergo further morphological transitions driven by curvature-induced depletion of wetting layers and subsequent coarsening of the surrounding domains, resulting in the breakup of target patterns into isolated domains of the matrix components. We find that domain coarsening slows down systematically as the number of components increases, while wetting accelerates it in all cases. The resulting morphologies and phase-separation pathways demonstrate how particle--component interactions can be used to control microstructural evolution in multicomponent mixtures, with potential implications for systems ranging from industrial materials to cellular biology.

AI.tldr: 2D phase-field simulations of surface-directed spinodal decomposition in N-component mixtures (N = 3, 4, 5) around a filler particle reveal lattice, droplet, and target/core-shell morphologies, with coarsening slowing as N increases and wetting accelerating it.
AI.motivation: The study aims to understand how particle-component interactions can control microstructural evolution in multicomponent mixtures, particularly during surface-directed spinodal decomposition where one phase acts as a filler particle and others phase separate around it.
AI.method: Two-dimensional phase-field simulations based on the Cahn-Hilliard description are used to model spinodal decomposition in N-component mixtures (N = 3, 4, 5). Both nonwetting and wetting conditions are investigated by varying interfacial tensions between the particle and other components, examining the competition between wetting kinetics and spinodal decomposition.
AI.result: Rich morphological evolution emerges, including lattice, droplet, and target (core-shell) morphologies. Target patterns consist of alternating component-rich rings around the particle. In intermediate-to-late times, curvature-induced depletion of wetting layers and coarsening cause target patterns to break up into isolated matrix domains. Domain coarsening slows systematically with increasing N, while wetting accelerates it in all cases.
AI.conclusion: The resulting morphologies and phase-separation pathways demonstrate that particle-component interactions can be used to control microstructural evolution in multicomponent mixtures, with potential implications for systems ranging from industrial materials to cellular biology.

title: Quantum geometry of collective pairing fluctuations in the superfluid weight of multiband superconductors
summary: Beyond the frozen-pairing contribution, the superfluid weight of a multiband superconductor contains a correction from the self-consistent relaxation of the pairing amplitudes under a phase twist. We show that this correction has a quantum-geometric origin, not in the space of Bloch states but in the space of collective pairing fields. For an attractive multiband Hubbard model at the mean-field level, the thermodynamic Hessian governing the pairing response coincides with the static Gaussian pair-fluctuation kernel at zero momentum at every temperature below $T_c$. Since gauge invariance relates a phase twist to a finite center-of-mass momentum of the pair field, the superfluid weight is set by the small-momentum curvature of the eigenvalue branch that evolves from the Goldstone mode, and the relaxation correction is a stiffness-weighted quantum metric of the corresponding soft eigenvector on the manifold of pairing configurations. The same construction yields the Ginzburg-Landau gradient coefficient with the identical geometric correction, hence the coherence-length tensor, and, with the low-frequency dynamics of the kernel, the pair-mass tensor. Lieb-lattice calculations verify the equivalence of the thermodynamic, fluctuation-kernel, and soft-mode formulations and the independence of the superfluid weight from the orbital embedding.

AI.tldr: The superfluid weight of a multiband superconductor includes a relaxation correction beyond frozen pairing, and this correction is shown to be a quantum-geometric quantity in the space of collective pairing fields rather than Bloch states.
AI.motivation: Conventional treatments of superfluid weight focus on the frozen-pairing contribution, leaving the self-consistent relaxation of pairing amplitudes under a phase twist poorly understood. This work seeks to identify the physical and mathematical origin of that relaxation correction.
AI.method: For an attractive multiband Hubbard model at mean-field level, the authors relate the thermodynamic Hessian governing pairing response to the static Gaussian pair-fluctuation kernel at zero momentum for all temperatures below Tc. Gauge invariance links a phase twist to a finite center-of-mass pair momentum, so the superfluid weight is extracted from the small-momentum curvature of the eigenvalue branch evolving from the Goldstone mode. The relaxation correction is expressed as a stiffness-weighted quantum metric of the corresponding soft eigenvector on the manifold of pairing configurations.
AI.result: The construction also produces the Ginzburg-Landau gradient coefficient with the same geometric correction, yielding the coherence-length tensor, and with the low-frequency kernel dynamics, the pair-mass tensor. Lieb-lattice calculations confirm the equivalence of thermodynamic, fluctuation-kernel, and soft-mode formulations, and show the superfluid weight is independent of orbital embedding.
AI.conclusion: The relaxation correction to superfluid weight has a quantum-geometric origin in the space of collective pairing fields, unifying thermodynamic, fluctuation, and soft-mode descriptions and enabling geometric access to coherence-length and pair-mass tensors.

title: Emergent Dimensionality in Diluted Power-Law Quantum Walks
summary: We investigate single-excitation quantum walks across the one-to-two-dimensional crossover in diluted power-law hopping models. Using arrays of $\ell$ coupled chains of length $L$, we identify the finite-size localization crossover from the longitudinal spreading of an initially localized excitation. The crossover filling is well described by an exponential approach to its two-dimensional value with increasing $\ell$, defining a characteristic transverse scale $\ell_e$, and effectively two-dimensional behavior emerges already for $\ell\ll L$. An independent spectral analysis shows that $\ell_e$ is set by the transverse extent of the eigenstates participating in the dynamics, providing a microscopic interpretation of the dimensional crossover. Our results reveal an intrinsic eigenstate scale governing emergent dimensionality in diluted systems with power-law hopping, a regime directly relevant to recently developed arrays of polar molecules, Rydberg atoms, and other quantum simulators with long-range interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies single-excitation quantum walks in diluted power-law hopping models, identifying a crossover from 1D to 2D behavior governed by a characteristic transverse scale set by eigenstate extent.
AI.motivation: Understanding how dimensionality emerges in disordered, long-range hopping systems is crucial for interpreting experiments with polar molecules, Rydberg atoms, and other quantum simulators.
AI.method: Arrays of $\ell$ coupled chains of length $L$ are analyzed via single-excitation quantum walks, examining longitudinal spreading of a localized excitation and performing independent spectral analysis of eigenstates.
AI.result: The finite-size localization crossover filling approaches its 2D value exponentially with increasing $\ell$; a characteristic transverse scale $\ell_e$ separates 1D and 2D regimes, and 2D behavior emerges for $\ell \ll L$. Spectral analysis shows $\ell_e$ is determined by the transverse extent of dynamically participating eigenstates.
AI.conclusion: An intrinsic eigenstate scale governs emergent dimensionality in diluted power-law hopping systems, relevant to long-range-interaction quantum simulators.

title: An associated model of Coulomb friction based on the real area of contact
summary: Coulomb friction is a non-associated law: it contains a threshold that depends on the contact pressure, i.e. a stress that is not conjugate to any internal variable, hence it admits no dissipation potential in the sense of generalized standard materials (GSM), and the incremental frictional contact problem is not a minimization problem. In this paper, we propose an alternative friction model that retains Coulomb-like behavior while being associated and fully GSM-compatible. Key to our formulation is the introduction of a new internal variable motivated by the microscopic contact state of rough surfaces, whose evolution is driven by the plastic deformation of the asperities. Under a non-decreasing contact pressure and below a threshold pressure, the model recovers Coulomb friction up to an asperity-scale penetration depth. This depth is physically meaningful and can be calibrated to reproduce known tribology results. Under decreasing contact pressures, the model exhibits a memory effect due to irreversible plastic deformation of the asperities, whereas above the pressure threshold it yields a saturation of the frictional traction. We present both penalty and Lagrange multiplier formulations of the model. A 2D finite element implementation of the penalty approach confirms excellent agreement with the classical Coulomb predictions across two benchmark tests.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an associated, GSM-compatible friction model that recovers Coulomb-like behavior via a new internal variable representing the microscopic contact state of rough asperities.
AI.motivation: Coulomb friction is non-associated: its threshold depends on contact pressure, a stress not conjugate to any internal variable, so it admits no dissipation potential in the GSM sense, and the incremental frictional contact problem is not a minimization problem. The authors aim to overcome this theoretical and computational obstacle.
AI.method: A new internal variable motivated by the microscopic contact state of rough surfaces is introduced, with evolution driven by plastic deformation of asperities. The model is formulated in both penalty and Lagrange multiplier versions, and a 2D finite element implementation of the penalty approach is developed.
AI.result: Under non-decreasing contact pressure and below a threshold pressure, the model recovers Coulomb friction up to an asperity-scale penetration depth, which is physically meaningful and calibratable against known tribology results. Under decreasing pressures it exhibits a memory effect from irreversible asperity plasticity, while above the pressure threshold the frictional traction saturates. The 2D FE penalty implementation shows excellent agreement with classical Coulomb predictions across two benchmark tests.
AI.conclusion: The proposed friction law retains Coulomb-like behavior while being associated and fully GSM-compatible, resolving the lack of a dissipation potential and the non-minimization nature of the incremental problem, with numerical validation confirming its accuracy.

title: Total-field atomic magnetometry using an elliptically-polarized frequency-modulated light beam for geomagnetic-field applications
summary: We investigate an all-optical scheme for high-sensitivity measurements of the Earth's scale magnetic field ($B$). The scheme is based on the Bell-Bloom technique with frequency-modulated light. A single elliptically polarized light beam is used both for pumping the alkali-metal atoms and probing Larmor precession of their spins under the external magnetic field. In contrast to many other high-sensitivity magnetometry schemes based on nonlinear polarization rotation of the light, the proposed approach enables the observation of magnetic resonance via changes in the light-beam ellipticity parameter. The approach has been validated in experiments with a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser, irradiating a $0.125$ cm$^3$ cesium vapor cell filled with a buffer gas. In the current experimental conditions, the achieved sensitivity is estimated at $220$ fT/$\surd$Hz under $B$$\,\approx\,$$50$ $μ$T, while the shot-noise floor corresponds to $\approx\,$$20$ fT/$\surd$Hz. The bandwidth is estimated at $\approx\,$$1$ kHz. The proposed simple and robust single-beam scheme is well suited for miniaturization and is therefore particularly promising for the development of compact, highly sensitive, low-power-consumption atomic magnetometers for a wide range of applications in the geomagnetic field.

AI.tldr: An all-optical, single-beam Bell-Bloom magnetometer with frequency-modulated light detects magnetic resonance via light ellipticity changes, reaching 220 fT/√Hz sensitivity at 50 µT.
AI.motivation: High-sensitivity magnetometry typically relies on nonlinear polarization rotation, which is complex and less suited to miniaturization. A simpler, robust scheme is needed for compact, low-power atomic magnetometers operating in the geomagnetic field range.
AI.method: Bell-Bloom technique with frequency-modulated light. A single elliptically polarized beam both pumps alkali atoms and probes Larmor spin precession. Magnetic resonance is observed through changes in the beam ellipticity parameter rather than nonlinear polarization rotation. Validated with a VCSEL irradiating a 0.125 cm³ cesium vapor cell with buffer gas.
AI.result: Sensitivity of 220 fT/√Hz at B ≈ 50 µT; shot-noise floor ≈ 20 fT/√Hz; bandwidth ≈ 1 kHz.
AI.conclusion: The simple, robust single-beam scheme is well suited to miniaturization and promising for compact, highly sensitive, low-power atomic magnetometers for geomagnetic-field applications.

title: Phase diagram and transition properties of the Blume-Capel model: A Monte Carlo study
summary: The Jx-Jy Blume-Capel model, with and without an external magnetic field, is investigated using the Monte Carlo method. Our aim is to verify the location of the tricritical point, examine the existence of reentrant behavior, and study the magnetocaloric properties of this specifically designed system. In the non-field case, the critical temperature given by the Monte Carlo simulations is lower compared to the conventional antiferromagnetic square lattice. When an external magnetic field is applied, we observed signs of a one-dimensional spontaneous symmetry-breaking phase in the mixed-states regime, which is counterintuitive with secondary specific-heat peak. We take the snapshot of this state and elucidated the underlying mechanisms using mean field theory in the field of spin-1 spinor Bose-Einstein condensate . Regarding reentrant behavior, we confirmed its occurrence as the magnetic field varies, but only when the temperature is kept constant. Temperature-dependent reentrant behavior could not be identified within this system. Finally, we examined the magnetocaloric properties and found no evidence of first-order phase transitions within the region of the considered phase-transition point. Although both inverse and direct magnetocaloric effects are present and related to the mixed state, we identified that the relevant phase transitions are all of the second order.

AI.tldr: Monte Carlo study of the Jx-Jy Blume-Capel model (with/without magnetic field) locates the tricritical point, examines reentrant behavior, and analyzes magnetocaloric properties; no first-order transitions found in the considered region.
AI.motivation: To verify the location of the tricritical point, examine the existence of reentrant behavior, and study the magnetocaloric properties of a specifically designed Jx-Jy Blume-Capel system.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulations of the Jx-Jy Blume-Capel model, with and without an external magnetic field; mean field theory in the context of spin-1 spinor Bose-Einstein condensate to interpret the observed mixed-state configuration.
AI.result: In the non-field case, the critical temperature is lower than that of the conventional antiferromagnetic square lattice. Under an applied field, signs of a one-dimensional spontaneous symmetry-breaking phase appear in the mixed-states regime, accompanied by a secondary specific-heat peak. Reentrant behavior occurs with varying magnetic field at constant temperature, but not as a temperature-dependent effect. Both inverse and direct magnetocaloric effects are present and tied to the mixed state; all relevant transitions are second order, with no evidence of first-order transitions.
AI.conclusion: The Jx-Jy Blume-Capel model exhibits reentrant behavior only under field variation at fixed temperature, and its relevant phase transitions in the studied region are exclusively second order despite coexisting inverse and direct magnetocaloric effects.

title: Many-body Interactions in Ultrafast Spectroscopy
summary: Nonlinear spectroscopy is widely used to probe ultrafast dynamics in matter. Signals of higher nonlinear orders encode valuable many-body dynamics but only recently have become individually retrievable. However, their physical interpretation in terms of double-sided Feynman diagrams is cumbersome and non-intuitive. Here, we establish an alternative framework that connects them to the underlying excitation conditions and many-body interactions. This approach predicts two classes of dynamic nonlinearities, due either to direct many-body interactions or to saturable kinetic channels. The method provides a direct physical interpretation of the retrieved signals, explaining their sign, magnitude, and dynamics. It also enables model-free reconstruction of the dynamics of a sub-ensemble of particles starting with a given number of excitons, which we demonstrate to be especially insightful. We validate the framework using colloidal CdSe/CdS core/shell quantum dots, which enable us to model nonlinearities of both classes in isolation and also combined.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an alternative framework to interpret higher-order nonlinear spectroscopic signals via excitation conditions and many-body interactions, replacing cumbersome double-sided Feynman diagram interpretation, and validates it in colloidal CdSe/CdS core/shell quantum dots.
AI.motivation: Higher-order nonlinear signals encode valuable many-body dynamics and have recently become individually retrievable, but their physical interpretation via double-sided Feynman diagrams is cumbersome and non-intuitive, creating a need for a more intuitive and physically transparent interpretive framework.
AI.method: The authors establish a framework linking higher-order nonlinear signals to underlying excitation conditions and many-body interactions. This framework predicts two classes of dynamic nonlinearities: those arising from direct many-body interactions and those from saturable kinetic channels. It also enables model-free reconstruction of the dynamics of a sub-ensemble of particles starting with a given number of excitons.
AI.result: The framework provides a direct physical interpretation of retrieved signals, explaining their sign, magnitude, and dynamics. It allows model-free reconstruction of sub-ensemble dynamics, which is demonstrated to be especially insightful. Validation is performed using colloidal CdSe/CdS core/shell quantum dots, where nonlinearities of both classes are modeled in isolation and in combination.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a direct, intuitive, and model-free approach to interpreting higher-order nonlinear spectroscopic signals, validated in quantum dots, and provides insight into many-body dynamics and sub-ensemble behavior.

title: Direct synthesis of moiré graphene with twist-tuned hybridization
summary: Twisted van der Waals (vdW) systems provide a powerful platform for exploring emergent correlated phenomena, including superconductivity, magnetism, and topological phases. The twist angle offers a continuous tuning parameter for modifying the underlying Hamiltonian, however, precise and reproducible control remains challenging. Existing approaches are limited by single-use device architectures, restricted angular precision, or vertical probing geometries. Here we introduce a reconfigurable graphene-based moiré platform in which two independently fabricated layers are mechanically assembled and rotated in situ using a micro-electromechanical system (MEMS). Raman spectroscopy confirms the formation and robustness of the twist-induced moiré potential and enables continuous, deterministic control of the twist angle. The moiré potential folds the electronic band structure and activates the longitudinal optical (LO) phonon mode, allowing us to map its dispersion and directly visualize the moiré momentum. Angle-dependent electronic band hybridization is resolved through the evolution of the double-resonant 2D mode. Near \(0^\circ\), an emergent asymmetry of the \(Γ\)-point G-mode phonon reveals phonon band folding and hybridization driven by the moiré superlattice potential and interlayer relaxation. Our platform provides a reproducible Raman reference for twisted bilayer graphene while eliminating device-to-device variability. More broadly, it establishes the twist angle as a deterministically controllable parameter for systematic studies of correlated and topological phenomena in moiré quantum materials.

AI.tldr: A reconfigurable MEMS-driven twisted bilayer graphene platform enables in situ, deterministic twist-angle control, with Raman spectroscopy mapping moiré-activated phonon dispersion, band folding, and interlayer relaxation near 0°.
AI.motivation: Twisted vdW systems are a powerful platform for correlated, magnetic, and topological phenomena, and the twist angle is a continuous tuning parameter of the Hamiltonian. However, existing methods suffer from single-use device architectures, limited angular precision, and vertical probing geometries, which restrict reproducible and systematic control.
AI.method: Two independently fabricated graphene layers are mechanically assembled and rotated in situ using a MEMS architecture, forming a reconfigurable moiré platform. Raman spectroscopy is used as the probe: the twist-induced moiré potential is confirmed and used to continuously and deterministically track the twist angle, fold the electronic band structure, activate the LO phonon mode, and resolve angle-dependent band hybridization via the double-resonant 2D mode.
AI.result: Raman measurements confirm the formation and robustness of the twist-induced moiré potential and enable continuous, deterministic twist-angle control. The moiré potential activates the LO phonon mode, allowing its dispersion to be mapped and the moiré momentum directly visualized. Angle-dependent electronic band hybridization is resolved through the 2D mode evolution, and near 0° an emergent asymmetry of the Γ-point G-mode reveals phonon band folding and hybridization driven by the moiré superlattice potential and interlayer relaxation.
AI.conclusion: The platform provides a reproducible Raman reference for twisted bilayer graphene while eliminating device-to-device variability. More broadly, it establishes the twist angle as a deterministically controllable parameter for systematic studies of correlated and topological phenomena in moiré quantum materials.

title: Heavy-fermion hybridization waves from Dirac spinons near a Kondo-breakdown quantum phase transition
summary: Motivated by the recent observation of spatially modulated screening in different paramagnetic heavy-fermion materials, we propose a theoretical mechanism for the emergence of such hybridization waves in frustrated Kondo lattices with no magnetic order. By applying a parton mean-field theory and a perturbative calculation to a minimal Kondo-Heisenberg lattice model, we demonstrate that a heavy Fermi liquid can naturally develop hybridization waves when it approaches a quantum phase transition where Kondo screening breaks down and the local magnetic moments form a Dirac spin liquid. We relate the strength of this mechanism to a kinematic condition on the electronic and spinon band structures and show that the spatial periodicity of the hybridization wave is set by a momentum $\vec{Q}$ connecting the nodes in the dispersion of the Dirac spinons to low-energy portions of the electronic band structure.

AI.tldr: This work proposes a theoretical mechanism for spatially modulated hybridization waves in frustrated, non-magnetically-ordered Kondo lattices, showing they emerge when a heavy Fermi liquid approaches a quantum phase transition into a Dirac spin liquid.
AI.motivation: Recent observations of spatially modulated screening in various paramagnetic heavy-fermion materials lack a clear theoretical explanation. This paper aims to provide a mechanism for the emergence of such hybridization waves in frustrated Kondo lattices without magnetic order.
AI.method: A parton mean-field theory combined with a perturbative calculation is applied to a minimal Kondo-Heisenberg lattice model.
AI.result: A heavy Fermi liquid can spontaneously develop hybridization waves as it approaches a quantum phase transition where Kondo screening breaks down and local moments form a Dirac spin liquid. The mechanism's strength is tied to a kinematic condition on the electronic and spinon band structures, and the spatial periodicity of the hybridization wave is determined by a momentum Q connecting Dirac spinon nodes to low-energy regions of the electronic band structure.
AI.conclusion: Spatially modulated hybridization waves are a natural consequence of a heavy Fermi liquid proximate to a Kondo-breakdown transition into a Dirac spin liquid, with their periodicity governed by the momentum separating spinon nodes and low-energy electronic states.

title: Characteristics of extinction behavior of ammonia partial cracking simulated fuels in counterflow premixed flames under lean condition
summary: In this study, the lean extinction behaviors of CH4 and a 16% cracked ammonia surrogate fuel, CR16, in counterflow premixed flames were compared. Experiments were conducted along with one-dimensional simulations using OPPDIF; the GRI-Mech 3.0 and UCSD mechanisms were applied to CH4 and CR16, respectively. CR16 exhibited higher extinction strain rates and resilience to strain-induced blow-out (RSIB) than those of CH4 under lean conditions. At Phi = 0.66, although both flames had the same extinction strain rate, CR16 showed a higher RSIB because of its longer flame time. Near its extinction, CR16 sustained H2 consumption, radical reactions, and heat release through the interflame region toward the stagnation plane. Hydrogen oxidation coupled with nitrogen-related pathways, including NH2 + NO and HNO reactions, supported this behavior. These results clarify the chemical basis for the superior extinction resistance of economically favorable low-cracking-ratio ammonia fuel.

AI.tldr: Lean extinction of CH4 and a 16% cracked ammonia surrogate (CR16) was compared in counterflow premixed flames via experiments and OPPDIF simulations, revealing CR16's superior strain resistance rooted in H2 and nitrogen-related chemistry.
AI.motivation: Ammonia is an economically favorable low-carbon fuel, but its combustion stability under lean, highly strained conditions is poorly understood. Comparing a cracked-ammonia surrogate with methane helps clarify the chemical basis for extinction resistance.
