AI.method: Lean extinction behaviors of CH4 and CR16 (16% cracked ammonia surrogate) were studied in counterflow premixed flames using experiments combined with one-dimensional OPPDIF simulations. GRI-Mech 3.0 was used for CH4 and the UCSD mechanism for CR16. Metrics included extinction strain rate and resilience to strain-induced blow-out (RSIB).
AI.result: CR16 showed higher extinction strain rates and greater RSIB than CH4 under lean conditions. At Phi = 0.66, both fuels had equal extinction strain rates, but CR16 exhibited higher RSIB due to longer flame time. Near extinction, CR16 sustained H2 consumption, radical reactions, and heat release across the interflame region toward the stagnation plane, supported by hydrogen oxidation coupled with nitrogen-related pathways (NH2 + NO and HNO reactions).
AI.conclusion: The superior extinction resistance of low-cracking-ratio ammonia fuel is chemically attributable to sustained H2 oxidation and nitrogen-related reaction pathways near extinction, clarifying the basis for the enhanced lean stability of economically favorable cracked ammonia fuels.

title: CrystalJev: thinking fast and slow with atomistic foundation models for materials discovery
comment: 43 pages, 6 main figures, 5 Extended Data figures, 1 Extended Data table; Supplementary Information included
summary: Atomistic foundation models triage millions of hypothetical materials but are used as slow simulators, their thresholded energies taken at face value. They are better read as fast decision-makers. CrystalJev queries a frozen interatomic potential once per unrelaxed structure and answers typed questions with calibrated probabilities, finite-sample guarantees and a rule for when to think slowly. Across 65 Matbench Discovery models, a 'stable' call is a probability in disguise, explained by a model's errors and the candidate population. Once trained, one forward pass decides nearly as well as a relaxation at a thirtieth of its cost, and a value-of-information theory sends slower computation only where decisions can change. The same layer answers electronic, mechanical and molecular questions. In a registered prospective test with 700 new density-functional calculations, single-pass forecasts calibrated only on existing data over-stated the stable fraction of unseen candidates (5.8%) by at most 2.1 percentage points.

AI.tldr: CrystalJev reframes frozen atomistic foundation models as fast, calibrated decision-makers rather than slow simulators: a single forward pass per unrelaxed structure yields typed answers with calibrated probabilities, finite-sample guarantees, and a value-of-information rule that allocates slow relaxation only where it can change decisions.
AI.motivation: Atomistic foundation models are already used to triage millions of hypothetical materials, but they are treated as slow simulators whose thresholded energies are taken at face value. A 'stable' call is in fact a probability in disguise, shaped by model errors and the candidate population. The paper argues these models are better read as fast decision-makers, and seeks a principled layer that turns their raw outputs into calibrated, decision-relevant answers.
AI.method: CrystalJev queries a frozen interatomic potential once per unrelaxed structure and returns typed answers with calibrated probabilities and finite-sample guarantees. It trains a calibration/decision layer that, once fitted, requires one forward pass, and applies a value-of-information theory to route slower computation only where decisions can change. The layer generalizes across electronic, mechanical, and molecular questions, and is evaluated across 65 Matbench Discovery models plus a registered prospective test with 700 new density-functional calculations.
AI.result: Across 65 Matbench Discovery models, a 'stable' call is revealed as a probability explained by the model's errors and the candidate population. After training, one forward pass decides nearly as well as a full relaxation at roughly a thirtieth of the cost, with slower computation sent only where it can alter decisions. In the prospective test, single-pass forecasts calibrated only on existing data overstated the stable fraction of unseen candidates (5.8%) by at most 2.1 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Frozen atomistic foundation models should be used as fast, calibrated decision-makers rather than slow simulators. CrystalJev offers a general layer providing calibrated probabilities, finite-sample guarantees, and cost-aware allocation of slower computation, and its prospective validation shows that single-pass forecasts stay within a bounded error on unseen candidates.

title: Soft Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Discovery of Phases of Matter
summary: A machine learning (ML) framework for phase-diagram construction in condensed matter systems with unknown phase structure is presented. The method combines physically motivated descriptors with contrastive representation learning and a two-stage data-generation workflow. First, a sparse set of configurations is generated by Monte Carlo simulated annealing in order to train a contrastive neural network that produces a low-dimensional embedding. Consequently, representative phase configurations are used as initial conditions for gradient-based optimization on a dense parameter grid, enabling efficient generation of refined datasets for high-resolution phase-diagram construction. In order to optimize the workflow, a variant of the method, in which derived descriptors are used as soft labels in the contrastive objective, is examined as well. The framework is demonstrated on a PbZrO3-inspired model potential formulated in terms of coupled order-parameter fields and used as a physically motivated testbed for exploring configuration diversity and phase behavior. The proposed approach provides a physically informed route to ML-assisted phase-diagram construction that integrates data analysis with adaptive dataset refinement.

AI.tldr: An ML framework combining physically motivated descriptors and contrastive representation learning with a two-stage data-generation workflow is proposed to construct phase diagrams of condensed matter systems with unknown phase structure.
AI.motivation: Phase-diagram construction in condensed matter systems is challenging when the phase structure is unknown. Conventional approaches require dense sampling over parameter space, which is computationally expensive. A physically informed, ML-assisted route is needed that integrates data analysis with adaptive dataset refinement.
AI.method: The method combines physically motivated descriptors with contrastive representation learning and a two-stage data-generation workflow. First, a sparse set of configurations is generated via Monte Carlo simulated annealing to train a contrastive neural network producing a low-dimensional embedding. Second, representative phase configurations serve as initial conditions for gradient-based optimization on a dense parameter grid, enabling efficient generation of refined datasets for high-resolution phase-diagram construction. A variant using derived descriptors as soft labels in the contrastive objective is also examined for workflow optimization.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on a PbZrO3-inspired model potential formulated in terms of coupled order-parameter fields, serving as a physically motivated testbed for exploring configuration diversity and phase behavior.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a physically informed route to ML-assisted phase-diagram construction that integrates data analysis with adaptive dataset refinement.

title: Graded Orbital Interface Engineering for Enhanced Damping-like Torque Efficiency
summary: Orbitronics has emerged as a promising approach for generating orbital currents using low cost, abundant materials through the orbital Hall effect. Since orbital current cannot directly interact with the local magnetization of a conventional ferromagnet, a non-magnetic layer with strong spin orbit coupling is required for converting orbital current into spin current. However, the propagation of orbital current across the interface between an orbital source and an orbital to spin converter remains poorly understood. Here, we tuned the Ru/Pt orbital interface from an abrupt interface to a graded interface by introducing a controlled RuPt intermixed layer and quantified the resulting damping like torque efficiencies. A small, intermixed thickness of 0.26 nm enhances the damping like torque efficiency by 15% compared with the abrupt Ru/Pt interface and by 70% compared with the Pt reference. Further increasing the intermixing thickness progressively suppresses the torque efficiency. We attribute this nonmonotonic behavior to the competition between enhanced orbital transmission through a gradual crystal field transition and orbital current dephasing due to alloy disorder and scattering. Our results demonstrate that the orbital-source/converter interface is an active element for controlling orbital transport and provides an experimentally accessible approach for optimizing orbital current transmission and torque generation in orbitronic heterostructures.

AI.tldr: Tuning the Ru/Pt orbital interface with a controlled RuPt intermixed layer reveals a nonmonotonic damping-like torque efficiency, peaking at 0.26 nm intermixing due to competition between enhanced orbital transmission and orbital dephasing.
AI.motivation: Orbital currents generated via the orbital Hall effect offer a low-cost route for orbitronics, but converting orbital current into spin current requires a non-magnetic layer with strong spin-orbit coupling. The propagation of orbital current across the orbital-source/converter interface remains poorly understood, limiting optimization of torque generation.
AI.method: The Ru/Pt orbital interface was tuned from abrupt to graded by introducing a controlled RuPt intermixed layer of varying thickness. The resulting damping-like torque efficiencies were quantified, and the nonmonotonic trend was interpreted in terms of orbital transmission and dephasing mechanisms.
AI.result: An intermixed thickness of 0.26 nm enhances the damping-like torque efficiency by 15% relative to the abrupt Ru/Pt interface and by 70% relative to the Pt reference. Increasing the intermixing thickness further progressively suppresses the torque efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The nonmonotonic behavior is attributed to competition between enhanced orbital transmission through a gradual crystal field transition and orbital current dephasing from alloy disorder and scattering. The orbital-source/converter interface is an active element for controlling orbital transport, providing an experimentally accessible approach to optimize orbital current transmission and torque generation in orbitronic heterostructures.

title: Time delay in nonadiabatic tunneling ionization
summary: The under-the-barrier recollision pathway during the tunneling ionization of an atom, despite its minuscule amplitude, leaves its signature on the observable photoelectron momentum distribution due to a phase shift relative to the direct ionization path, that can be interpreted as a tunneling time delay. We investigate how this time delay is modified in the nonadiabatic regime, where the tunneling barrier evolves dynamically during the ionization process. Our analysis is based on a simple model of a one-dimensional short-range potential driven by a strong laser pulse which remains amenable to a systematic analytical treatment with the strong field approximation (SFA). We show a significant contribution of the high-order SFA corrections, which describes the recollision channel with recombination and further ionization, and is additional to the rescattering. Whereas the recombination channel dominates over the rescattering for the tunneling time delay in the quasistatic regime at relatively large laser fields, their contributions are reversed in weak fields.

AI.tldr: The under-the-barrier recollision pathway in tunneling ionization imprints a tunneling time delay on photoelectron momentum distributions; this delay is analyzed in the nonadiabatic regime using a 1D short-range potential within high-order SFA, showing the recombination channel dominates in strong quasistatic fields while rescattering dominates in weak fields.
AI.motivation: The under-the-barrier recollision pathway, though of tiny amplitude, affects observable photoelectron momentum distributions via a phase shift relative to direct ionization, interpretable as a tunneling time delay. How this delay changes in the nonadiabatic regime—where the tunneling barrier evolves dynamically—is not well understood.
AI.method: A simple one-dimensional short-range potential driven by a strong laser pulse is used, remaining amenable to systematic analytical treatment with the strong field approximation (SFA), including high-order SFA corrections that describe the recollision channel with recombination and further ionization, in addition to rescattering.
AI.result: High-order SFA corrections contribute significantly to the tunneling time delay. In the quasistatic regime at relatively large laser fields the recombination channel dominates the delay, whereas in weak fields the contributions of recombination and rescattering are reversed.
AI.conclusion: The tunneling time delay from under-the-barrier recollision is sensitively modified in the nonadiabatic regime, with the relative weight of recombination and rescattering channels depending on laser field strength, underscoring the importance of high-order SFA corrections.

title: Long-Range Nonequilibrium Correlations as a Thermodynamic Speedometer
summary: Despite purely local microscopic dynamics, nonequilibrium steady states can develop long-range correlations. We investigate this phenomenon in the boundary-driven symmetric simple exclusion process by relating its exact nonlocal large-deviation functional to finite-time thermodynamic irreversibility under weak time-dependent driving. Decomposing the long-range correlations into hydrodynamic modes, we find that the lag associated with the slowest mode satisfies an upper bound determined by the excess entropy production rate at each driving frequency. This bound is approached in the quasistatic limit, whereas progressively shorter-wavelength modes do not generally satisfy the corresponding bound. These results provide a quantitative connection between the curvature of the large-deviation functional, long-range correlations in the nonequilibrium steady state, and finite-time dissipation. Within the linear-response regime considered here, they indicate that the longest-wavelength hydrodynamic mode has a distinct relation between slow relaxation and thermodynamic irreversibility.

AI.tldr: The paper links long-range correlations in a boundary-driven symmetric simple exclusion process to finite-time thermodynamic irreversibility by relating the exact nonlocal large-deviation functional to weak time-dependent driving, showing that the slowest hydrodynamic mode's lag is bounded by the excess entropy production rate.
AI.motivation: Nonequilibrium steady states can exhibit long-range correlations despite purely local microscopic dynamics, and the relationship between these correlations, the curvature of the large-deviation functional, and finite-time dissipation is not quantitatively understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze the boundary-driven symmetric simple exclusion process, linking its exact nonlocal large-deviation functional to finite-time thermodynamic irreversibility under weak time-dependent driving, and decompose the long-range correlations into hydrodynamic modes.
AI.result: The lag associated with the slowest hydrodynamic mode satisfies an upper bound set by the excess entropy production rate at each driving frequency; this bound is approached in the quasistatic limit, while progressively shorter-wavelength modes generally do not satisfy the corresponding bound.
AI.conclusion: A quantitative connection is established between the curvature of the large-deviation functional, long-range correlations in the nonequilibrium steady state, and finite-time dissipation. Within the linear-response regime, the longest-wavelength hydrodynamic mode exhibits a distinct relation between slow relaxation and thermodynamic irreversibility.

title: Coupled cluster theory for multireference and open-shell molecules
summary: We introduce a simple coupled cluster approach for multireference and open-shell systems. In the restricted active space coupled cluster framework, the cluster operator only includes excitations from doubly occupied to virtual orbitals, and this ensures the individual operators commute among each other. The ground and excited states are obtained by diagonalisation of the coupled cluster similarity transformed Hamiltonian in a restricted active space. We demonstrate the framework for the RAS-CCSD model, where single and double excitations are included in the cluster operator, and likewise for a complete active space. We consider systems with multireference character and open-shell systems in a spin-adapted manner. The approach captures significantly more dynamical correlation than without the coupled cluster similarity transformation.

AI.tldr: A simple coupled cluster approach (RAS-CC) is introduced for multireference and open-shell systems, where the cluster operator contains only doubly occupied to virtual excitations so that individual operators commute. States are obtained by diagonalizing the similarity-transformed Hamiltonian in a restricted active space, demonstrated at the CCSD level.
AI.motivation: Multireference and open-shell systems are challenging for standard single-reference coupled cluster methods, which struggle with strong static correlation. A framework is needed that handles multireference character and open shells while still capturing dynamical correlation.
AI.method: In the restricted active space coupled cluster (RAS-CC) framework, the cluster operator includes only excitations from doubly occupied to virtual orbitals, ensuring the individual operators commute among each other. Ground and excited states are obtained by diagonalization of the coupled cluster similarity-transformed Hamiltonian within a restricted active space. The framework is demonstrated for the RAS-CCSD model, with single and double excitations in the cluster operator, and likewise for a complete active space; systems are treated in a spin-adapted manner.
AI.result: The approach is demonstrated for RAS-CCSD and the complete active space variant, applied to systems with multireference character and open-shell systems. It captures significantly more dynamical correlation than without the coupled cluster similarity transformation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RAS-CC framework offers a simple, spin-adapted route to treat multireference and open-shell systems, with the similarity transformation providing substantially improved dynamical correlation over the bare active space treatment.

title: Sparse qubit operation in a 6$\times$6 quantum dot array
comment: Main: 11 pages, 5 figures. Supplementary Information: 17 pages
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires increasing the qubit count while maintaining high performance and connectivity. Semiconductor qubits have demonstrated high-fidelity operation, but growing the system size at sufficient connectivity remains challenging, such that scaling mainly occurred in one spatial direction to preserve access for control lines in the other. Here, we realise an approach that relaxes the requirements on fabrication and demonstrate a 6$\times$6 quantum dot array, defined by a shared barrier gate and individual plunger gates. The quantum dots are tuned through coherent spin shuttling over distances up to 5.2um into a sparse configuration of 10 simultaneously operated qubits, leaving space for shuttling connections. We reduce crosstalk by 42$\times$ in this separated regime, enabling high-fidelity simultaneous single-qubit control, while control-Z operations can be implemented through shuttling and plunger-only control. These results promise high-connectivity quantum circuits, enabled by scaling to two-dimensional geometries and exploiting shuttling.

AI.tldr: The paper realizes a 6x6 semiconductor quantum dot array defined by a shared barrier gate and individual plunger gates, using coherent spin shuttling to tune dots into a sparse 10-qubit configuration with reduced crosstalk and high-fidelity control.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation demands increasing qubit count while maintaining high performance and connectivity. Semiconductor qubits achieve high-fidelity operation, but scaling system size at sufficient connectivity is difficult; growth has mainly occurred in one spatial dimension to preserve control-line access in the other direction. A new approach is needed to relax fabrication constraints and enable two-dimensional scaling.
AI.method: The authors fabricate a 6x6 quantum dot array defined by a shared barrier gate and individual plunger gates. Quantum dots are tuned via coherent spin shuttling over distances up to 5.2 um into a sparse configuration of 10 simultaneously operated qubits, leaving space for shuttling connections. Crosstalk is reduced by 42x in this separated regime, enabling high-fidelity simultaneous single-qubit control, with control-Z operations implemented through shuttling and plunger-only control.
AI.result: A 6x6 quantum dot array was demonstrated with dots tuned by coherent spin shuttling up to 5.2 um into a sparse 10-qubit configuration. Crosstalk was reduced by 42x in the separated regime, enabling high-fidelity simultaneous single-qubit control, and control-Z operations were implemented via shuttling and plunger-only control.
AI.conclusion: These results promise high-connectivity quantum circuits, enabled by scaling to two-dimensional geometries and exploiting shuttling.

title: Chiral Parafermions in Floquet $\mathbb{Z}_N$ Topological Order
summary: Floquet topological order (FTO) extends topology beyond equilibrium, giving rise to phenomena, such as the dynamical transmutation of anyons. Here, we realize $\mathbb{Z}_N$ FTO in a generalized Kitaev honeycomb model with clock degrees of freedom using a three-step periodic drive. The driven system admits an emergent description in terms of constrained parafermions coupled to conserved $\mathbb{Z}_N$ gauge fields. At the boundary, the drive generates chiral parafermionic Floquet edge modes. We resolve their propagation through correlation functions, characterize their fractional quantum-information transport through the radical chiral unitary index, and use their dynamics to probe exchange statistics. In the bulk, we explore the dynamical anyon transmutation with a non-equilibrium loop order parameter. At a Floquet sweet spot, where the drive becomes Clifford, these phenomena can be accessed using stabilizer simulations. Short-time matrix-product-state simulations away from this point show that the chiral edge response persists at accessible times. Our results establish $\mathbb{Z}_N$ Kitaev models as a setting for exploring intrinsically non-equilibrium topological phenomena on qudit-based quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper realizes Z_N Floquet topological order in a periodically driven generalized Kitaev honeycomb model with clock degrees of freedom, exhibiting chiral parafermionic edge modes and dynamical anyon transmutation.
AI.motivation: Floquet topological order extends topology beyond equilibrium and enables phenomena such as dynamical transmutation of anyons, motivating its realization in a controllable qudit-based setting.
AI.method: A three-step periodic drive is applied to a generalized Kitaev honeycomb model with clock degrees of freedom. The driven system is described via constrained parafermions coupled to conserved Z_N gauge fields. Edge correlations, the radical chiral unitary index, and exchange statistics probe the edge modes, while a non-equilibrium loop order parameter probes bulk transmutation. Stabilizer simulations are used at a Clifford Floquet sweet spot, and short-time matrix-product-state simulations are used away from it.
AI.result: The drive generates chiral parafermionic Floquet edge modes. Their propagation is resolved through correlation functions, their fractional quantum-information transport is characterized by the radical chiral unitary index, and their exchange statistics are probed dynamically. Bulk dynamical anyon transmutation is captured by a non-equilibrium loop order parameter. At the Floquet sweet spot, these phenomena are accessible via stabilizer simulations; away from it, short-time MPS simulations show the chiral edge response persists at accessible times.
AI.conclusion: Z_N Kitaev models establish a viable setting for exploring intrinsically non-equilibrium topological phenomena on qudit-based quantum processors.

title: A pressure-based coupled general synthetic iterative scheme for rarefied gas flow simulation
summary: This work develops a pressure-based coupled (PBC) GSIS. Within each GSIS iteration, a conventional kinetic solver advances the velocity distribution function, from which non-equilibrium constitutive relations are extracted. A PBC macroscopic solver then solves the steady macroscopic synthetic equations: continuity and momentum equations are solved as a coupled pressure-velocity system under fixed temperature, followed by a segregated temperature solve. A boundary treatment is constructed to maintain strict consistency between kinetic boundary fluxes and macroscopic boundary conditions throughout the macroscopic iterations. The proposed method is validated against direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) data across multiple three-dimensional test cases, including tube-to-vacuum flows, a dynamic gas lock configuration for EUV lithography, divertors in nuclear fusion, and sphere flow at Mach numbers up to 10. Numerical results demonstrate that our GSIS-PBC preserves asymptotic-preserving properties and yields satisfactory accuracy across continuum-to-transitional flow regimes. For low-speed near-continuum internal flows, GSIS-PBC delivers wall clock time speed-ups of up to two orders of magnitude compared with the conventional iterative scheme, and substantially outperforms the original density-based GSIS for challenging low-Mach internal flow problems. For nuclear-fusion divertor flows, GSIS-PBC is faster than the DSMC by four orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: This work develops a pressure-based coupled (PBC) GSIS that couples pressure-velocity in the macroscopic solver with a boundary treatment ensuring kinetic-macroscopic consistency. Validated against DSMC on 3D cases, it preserves asymptotic-preserving properties and achieves up to 2 orders of magnitude speed-up over conventional iterative schemes and 4 orders over DSMC.
AI.motivation: Existing GSIS methods (e.g., density-based GSIS) struggle with challenging low-Mach internal flow problems, and improved efficiency/robustness is needed for continuum-to-transitional flows, particularly low-speed near-continuum internal flows and applications like nuclear-fusion divertors.
AI.method: Develops a pressure-based coupled (PBC) GSIS. Each GSIS iteration uses a conventional kinetic solver to advance the velocity distribution function and extract non-equilibrium constitutive relations; a PBC macroscopic solver then solves steady macroscopic synthetic equations—continuity and momentum equations as a coupled pressure-velocity system under fixed temperature, followed by a segregated temperature solve. A boundary treatment maintains strict consistency between kinetic boundary fluxes and macroscopic boundary conditions across macroscopic iterations.
AI.result: Validated against DSMC across multiple 3D test cases (tube-to-vacuum flows, a dynamic gas lock for EUV lithography, nuclear-fusion divertors, sphere flow at Mach up to 10). Preserves asymptotic-preserving properties with satisfactory accuracy across continuum-to-transitional regimes. For low-speed near-continuum internal flows, achieves up to two orders of magnitude wall-clock speed-up over the conventional iterative scheme and substantially outperforms the original density-based GSIS for low-Mach internal flows; for divertor flows, four orders of magnitude faster than DSMC.
AI.conclusion: GSIS-PBC is an efficient, accurate, and asymptotically-preserving method for continuum-to-transitional flows, with substantial computational advantages over conventional iterative schemes, density-based GSIS, and DSMC.

title: Identifying Plastic Inorganic Semiconductors Requires More Rigorous Criteria
summary: The identification of plastic inorganic semiconductors becomes challenging when their mechanical responses depend on crystallographic orientation, sample size, and loading conditions. Using layered GeSe as a model system, we examine its deformation behavior through macroscopic compression, bending, conventional micropillar compression, and eccentric micropillar compression. Under macroscopic compression perpendicular to the layers, GeSe sustains approximately 23% strain without fracture, whereas bending along the c-axis armchair direction produces brittle cleavage fracture. Conventional micropillar compression results in brittle fragmentation, while eccentric loading introduces a shear component that activates pronounced interlayer sliding and accommodates deformation. These contrasting responses reflect the coupled effects of bonding topology, interlayer van der Waals interactions, defect density, stress constraints, and strain path on the competition between sliding and fracture. The results highlight the limitations of identifying plasticity from a single direction, scale, or test and support a systematic evaluation framework combining multiple directions, length scales, loading modes, and characterization techniques. More rigorous and unified criteria are needed to guide reliable materials selection for flexible electronics and devices integrated on curved surfaces.

AI.tldr: Using layered GeSe, the study shows that plastic vs. brittle behavior in inorganic semiconductors depends jointly on crystallographic orientation, sample size, and loading mode, so plasticity cannot be judged from a single test.
AI.motivation: Identifying plastic inorganic semiconductors is difficult because mechanical responses vary with crystallographic orientation, sample size, and loading conditions, making single-condition assessments unreliable for applications such as flexible electronics and curved-surface devices.
AI.method: Layered GeSe was used as a model system and tested via macroscopic compression, bending, conventional micropillar compression, and eccentric micropillar compression.
AI.result: Macroscopic compression perpendicular to layers sustained ~23% strain without fracture; bending along the c-axis armchair direction gave brittle cleavage fracture; conventional micropillar compression caused brittle fragmentation; eccentric loading introduced shear that activated pronounced interlayer sliding and accommodated deformation.
AI.conclusion: Plasticity identification requires a systematic framework combining multiple directions, length scales, loading modes, and characterization techniques; more rigorous, unified criteria are needed for reliable materials selection in flexible electronics and curved-surface devices.

title: Classifications in modular restricted Boltzmann machines
summary: We consider a modular associative neural network made of $L$ Hopfield models (HMs), coupled so that intra-module interactions are Hebbian and inter-module interactions are anti-Hebbian; this competitive coupling is known to endow the network with pattern-disentanglement capabilities. The integral representation of this system coincides with an assembly of $L$ restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) whose hidden layers are coupled, thereby extending the HM-RBM duality to the modular setting. We then train this modular RBM, via one-step contrastive divergence, to perform a classification task in which a query encoded on the visible layers is mapped onto an $L$-tuple of labels read off the hidden layers. When the query is composed of $L$ patterns that are mutually orthogonal on average, we prove that the RBM weights obtained as empirical means over the training dataset, as suggested by the HM-RBM equivalence, constitute a fixed point of the learning dynamics, and we derive an explicit, non-asymptotic bound on the residual drift. We then turn to a harder classification task in which each module is queried with a mixture of $L$ patterns and we show numerically that the same setting for the RBM weights still provides an effective set-up, letting the network jointly classify and disentangle the mixture.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a modular associative network of L coupled Hopfield models with Hebbian intra-module and anti-Hebbian inter-module interactions, whose integral representation is a coupled assembly of L restricted Boltzmann machines. It extends the Hopfield-RBM duality to a modular setting and analyzes training via one-step contrastive divergence for classification and mixture disentanglement.
AI.motivation: Competitive coupling among Hopfield modules is known to provide pattern-disentanglement capabilities, but a unified statistical-mechanical and learning-theoretic treatment of such modular systems, especially through the Hopfield-RBM duality, was lacking. The paper aims to extend this duality to the modular case and to understand whether the resulting weights, suggested by the equivalence, are stable under a practical learning rule.
AI.method: The authors construct a modular associative network of L Hopfield models with Hebbian intra-module and anti-Hebbian inter-module couplings, and map its integral representation onto an assembly of L RBMs with coupled hidden layers. They train this modular RBM with one-step contrastive divergence on a classification task, where a visible-layer query is mapped to an L-tuple of labels read from the hidden layers.
AI.result: For queries composed of L patterns that are mutually orthogonal on average, the paper proves that the RBM weights given by empirical means over the training dataset, as suggested by the Hopfield-RBM equivalence, form a fixed point of the learning dynamics, and derives an explicit non-asymptotic bound on the residual drift. For a harder task where each module receives a mixture of L patterns, numerical experiments show that the same weight setting remains effective, allowing the network to jointly classify and disentangle the mixture.
AI.conclusion: The Hopfield-RBM duality extends naturally to modular networks, and the equivalence-suggested empirical-mean weights are provably near-fixed points for orthogonal-average queries with a non-asymptotic drift bound. The same setting also works empirically for mixture queries, enabling joint classification and disentanglement.

title: Heterogeneous diffusion with recruitment and mortality
summary: We study a heterogeneous diffusion process with a position-dependent diffusion coefficient in the presence of independent recruitment and mortality. This framework generalises heterogeneous diffusion under stochastic resetting, which is recovered as the special case of equal recruitment and mortality rates. At long times, the system approaches a non-equilibrium stationary state with a mean squared displacement that saturates to a value independent of the recruitment rate. Crucially, this saturation limit directly encodes the underlying transport regime via an effective exponent applied to the diffusion coefficient, and we characterise the non-trivial transition to this stationary regime. We further derive the mean first-passage time to a target and show that, for a fixed recruitment-to-mortality ratio, an optimal mortality rate minimises the search time. This "mortality-assisted search" effect is confirmed by numerical evaluation. Reinterpreting recruitment and mortality as infection and removal processes, we apply the model to epidemic spreading and show that a moderate removal rate can counter-intuitively accelerate, rather than delay, the arrival of infection at a new spatial region. Beyond epidemiology, our framework offers broad relevance to systems featuring concurrent particle creation and destruction, such as bacterial growth, tracer diffusion in reactive fluids, or cellular population dynamics in crowded environments.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes heterogeneous diffusion with position-dependent diffusivity under independent recruitment (creation) and mortality (destruction), generalizing stochastic-resetting diffusion. It finds a non-equilibrium stationary state where the MSD saturates independent of the recruitment rate but whose saturation value encodes the transport regime via an effective exponent, characterizes the transition, derives the mean first-passage time, and shows an optimal mortality rate minimizes search time — an effect also applied to epidemic spreading.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous diffusion under stochastic resetting is a well-studied framework, but real systems (bacterial growth, reactive fluids, cellular populations) involve concurrent particle creation and destruction rather than simple resetting. The authors aim to generalize the resetting picture to independent recruitment and mortality and to understand how these competing processes shape stationary statistics, first-passage properties, and search efficiency.
AI.method: The authors formulate a heterogeneous diffusion process with a position-dependent diffusion coefficient subject to independent recruitment and mortality rates. They recover stochastic resetting as the special case of equal rates, compute the long-time non-equilibrium stationary state and mean squared displacement (MSD), analyze the saturation value and its encoding of the transport regime through an effective exponent, characterize the transition to the stationary regime, derive the mean first-passage time to a target, and identify an optimal mortality rate minimizing search time. Numerical evaluation confirms the analytical results, and the model is reinterpreted with infection and removal processes for epidemics.
AI.result: At long times the system reaches a non-equilibrium stationary state whose MSD saturates to a value independent of the recruitment rate. This saturation limit directly encodes the transport regime via an effective exponent applied to the diffusion coefficient, and the non-trivial transition to the stationary regime is characterized. For a fixed recruitment-to-mortality ratio, an optimal mortality rate minimizes the mean first-passage (search) time, confirmed numerically. In the epidemic interpretation, a moderate removal rate can counter-intuitively accelerate rather than delay the arrival of infection at a new spatial region.
AI.conclusion: The framework generalizes heterogeneous diffusion under stochastic resetting to independent recruitment and mortality, yielding a non-equilibrium stationary state whose saturation MSD encodes the transport regime and producing a mortality-assisted search effect with an optimal mortality rate. It offers broad relevance to systems with concurrent particle creation and destruction, including bacterial growth, tracer diffusion in reactive fluids, cellular population dynamics in crowded environments, and epidemic spreading.

title: What Rate Theories Compute: Chemical kinetics from Arrhenius to machine-learned potentials
comment: Review article. 41 pages: 31-page main manuscript and 10-page Supplementary Materials; 2 tables and 1 graphical abstract
summary: Major advances in chemical rate theory changed what was computed and what a barrier meant. I organize this conceptual history around those changes, while retaining the controlled corrections and limiting relations between theories. The calculated quantities include an empirical rate constant, a collision count, a thermodynamic activation free energy, a statistical flux across a dividing surface, a stochastic escape rate, an energy-resolved microcanonical rate, a quantum flux correlation function, and an ensemble of reactive paths computed with electronic-structure or machine-learned potentials. I compare the assumptions with the limits stated by the pioneering authors. A rate constant is inferred from measurements under a stated rate law; its temperature dependence defines an apparent activation energy $E_a$. Activation free energy $ΔG^{\ddagger}$, activation enthalpy $ΔH^{\ddagger}$, activation entropy $ΔS^{\ddagger}$, the prefactor, transmission coefficient $κ$, and saddle height require a kinetic model and, where relevant, a standard state, dividing surface, ensemble, and dynamical correction for their interpretation in a rate calculation. In hydrogen transfer by soybean lipoxygenase-1, similar single-isotope activation parameters accompany a large change in isotope-sensitive dynamics. Five rate benchmarks illustrate the errors different comparisons test and motivate seven reporting items. These distinctions guide comparisons of rates and interpretations of activation parameters.

AI.tldr: This conceptual history traces how advances in chemical rate theory redefined what is computed and what a "barrier" means, organizing the changing calculated quantities—from empirical rate constants to quantum flux correlation functions and machine-learned reactive path ensembles—around controlled corrections and limiting relations between theories.
AI.motivation: Rate theory's evolution changed both the computed quantities and the meaning of a barrier, yet comparisons between theories and measurements often conflate quantities governed by different assumptions, limiting conditions, and reference states. A conceptual account is needed to clarify these distinctions and guide valid rate comparisons and activation-parameter interpretations.
AI.method: The author organizes the conceptual history around the changing calculated quantities and retains the controlled corrections and limiting relations linking successive theories. Assumptions are compared with the limits stated by pioneering authors. Distinct computed objects are catalogued: empirical rate constant, collision count, thermodynamic activation free energy, statistical flux across a dividing surface, stochastic escape rate, energy-resolved microcanonical rate, quantum flux correlation function, and ensembles of reactive paths from electronic-structure or machine-learned potentials.

Interpreting ΔG‡, ΔH‡, ΔS‡, the prefactor, transmission coefficient κ, and saddle height requires a kinetic model and, where relevant, a standard state, dividing surface, ensemble, and dynamical correction.
