title: Bichargon Hall Effect
summary: The conventional Hall effect arises from the transverse deflection of mobile electronic charge carriers in conductors. Here, we predict a bosonic charge Hall effect in charge-ordered insulators mediated by bichargons, collective bosonic excitations of charge order carrying quantized electric charges $\pm 2e$. In contrast to conventional electronic carriers, a thermally excited bichargon gas does not support dc electrical conduction in response to an external electric field despite its constituents carrying finite electric charges. We show that a temperature gradient can instead drive a diffusive flow of thermal bichargons, while an out-of-plane magnetic field deflects the oppositely charged bichargons in opposite transverse directions via the Lorentz force, leading to a finite Hall charge current and opposite charge accumulations at the sample edges. Our results broaden the paradigm of charge Hall transport beyond conventional electronic conductors, establishing that a charge Hall response can emerge in an electrically \emph{insulating} system through charged bosonic quasiparticles.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts a bosonic charge Hall effect in charge-ordered insulators, where thermally excited bichargons (charge-±2e bosonic excitations) driven by a temperature gradient are transversely deflected by a magnetic field, producing a finite Hall charge current and edge charge accumulation despite the system being electrically insulating.
AI.motivation: The conventional Hall effect relies on transverse deflection of mobile electronic charge carriers in conductors. The authors aim to extend the paradigm of charge Hall transport beyond conventional electronic conductors by asking whether a charge Hall response can arise in an electrically insulating system via charged bosonic quasiparticles.
AI.method: The authors theoretically predict and analyze a bosonic charge Hall effect mediated by bichargons—collective bosonic excitations of charge order carrying quantized charges ±2e. They examine the response of a thermally excited bichargon gas to external electric fields and temperature gradients in the presence of an out-of-plane magnetic field, invoking the Lorentz force on oppositely charged bichargons.
AI.result: Unlike conventional electronic carriers, the thermally excited bichargon gas does not support dc electrical conduction under an external electric field despite its constituents carrying finite charges. However, a temperature gradient drives a diffusive flow of thermal bichargons, and an out-of-plane magnetic field deflects oppositely charged bichargons in opposite transverse directions via the Lorentz force, yielding a finite Hall charge current and opposite charge accumulations at the sample edges.
AI.conclusion: The results broaden the paradigm of charge Hall transport beyond conventional electronic conductors, establishing that a charge Hall response can emerge in an electrically insulating system through charged bosonic quasiparticles.

title: Local-moment magnets on all close-packed lattices are equivalent
summary: The Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the fcc lattice is a canonical example of frustration. The fcc lattice is but one of an infinite number of close-packed structures, all of which have the same frustration-inducing local geometry. In this letter, we demonstrate a hidden symmetry that relates classical magnets on all close-packed lattices. This symmetry derives from a similar property in tight binding models that may explain the disordered low-temperature structures of lithium and sodium metals. In magnets, the symmetry holds when couplings are restricted to nearest ($J_1$) and next-nearest neighbours ($J_2$). It guarantees that all close-packed lattices are equivalent at the Luttinger-Tisza level. For any given values of $J_1$ and $J_2$, they have the same ground-state energy. Their ground state momenta are identical when projected onto the stacking plane. We construct a unified phase diagram as a function of $J_1$ and $J_2$ couplings for Heisenberg, XY and Ising magnets on any close-packed lattice. In each phase, the ground-state degeneracy is the same on all close-packed lattices, even after accounting for multi-Q spirals. This phase diagram can be easily adapted to any magnet composed of stacked triangular layers with similar couplings. Fluctuations above the classical ground state(s) are not related by any symmetry. This suggests that close-packed structures can show interesting differences in order-by-disorder selection.

AI.tldr: A hidden symmetry relates classical magnets on all close-packed lattices with J1-J2 couplings, giving a unified phase diagram and equal degeneracies.
AI.motivation: The Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the fcc lattice is a canonical frustration example, and fcc is only one of infinitely many close-packed structures sharing the same frustration-inducing local geometry. The authors aim to reveal a symmetry tying classical magnets on all close-packed lattices together.
AI.method: The symmetry derives from an analogous property in tight-binding models (potentially explaining disordered low-T structures of Li and Na metals). It holds for magnets with nearest (J1) and next-nearest (J2) neighbor couplings, and is analyzed at the Luttinger-Tisza level, with a unified phase diagram constructed for Heisenberg, XY, and Ising magnets on any close-packed lattice.
AI.result: The symmetry guarantees all close-packed lattices are equivalent at the Luttinger-Tisza level: for given J1, J2 they share the same ground-state energy, and identical ground-state momenta when projected onto the stacking plane. Ground-state degeneracy is the same across all close-packed lattices in each phase, even accounting for multi-Q spirals.
AI.conclusion: The unified phase diagram can be adapted to any magnet of stacked triangular layers with similar couplings. Since fluctuations above the classical ground state(s) are not related by any symmetry, close-packed structures may exhibit interesting differences in order-by-disorder selection.

title: Neural-Operator-Predicted Time-Dependent Reduced Subspaces for Projection-Based Simulation of Nonlinear PDEs
summary:
Accurate numerical simulation of nonlinear partial differential equation initial value problems typically requires high-dimensional full-order discretizations at substantial computational cost. While purely data-driven surrogates can speed up prediction, these "black box" approximations do not necessarily satisfy the governing equations during inference. In this paper we present a hybrid framework, which combines neural operators with projection-based reduced-order modeling for nonlinear PDE simulation. The key idea is to train a neural operator to map the initial condition to a time-dependent reduced subspace, and then evolve low-dimensional reduced coordinates by solving the governing dynamical equations projected on this learned moving trial subspace. In this way, the network predicts an adaptive reduced representation rather than the full trajectory directly, while the online solver preserves a physics-based reduced evolution.
  We test this method on two representative nonlinear PDEs: the viscous Burgers' equation and the Fisher--KPP reaction--diffusion equation. In both cases, the proposed approach achieves successful reduced-order simulation with substantial wall-clock speedup relative to the corresponding full-order solver while maintaining relative errors on the order of \(10^{-2}\) to \(10^{-1}\) across the tested resolutions. These results demonstrate that a low-dimensional learned time-dependent reduced subspace can be used to predict solutions to nonlinear PDEs while retaining the advantages of projection-based reduced dynamics. Overall, this method provides a promising framework for fast and physically grounded data-assisted simulation of nonlinear PDEs.

AI.tldr: Combines neural operators with projection-based reduced-order modeling: a network maps initial conditions to a time-dependent reduced subspace, and reduced coordinates are evolved by projecting the governing equations onto this learned moving subspace.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity simulation of nonlinear PDE initial value problems requires costly high-dimensional discretizations, while purely data-driven surrogates are black-box and may not satisfy the governing equations during inference.
AI.method: A hybrid framework trains a neural operator to map the initial condition to a time-dependent reduced subspace; low-dimensional reduced coordinates are then evolved by solving the governing dynamical equations projected onto this learned moving trial subspace, yielding an adaptive reduced representation instead of a direct full-trajectory prediction.
AI.result: Tested on the viscous Burgers' equation and the Fisher--KPP reaction--diffusion equation, the method achieves successful reduced-order simulation with substantial wall-clock speedup over full-order solvers while maintaining relative errors on the order of 10^-2 to 10^-1 across tested resolutions.
AI.conclusion: A low-dimensional learned time-dependent reduced subspace can predict nonlinear PDE solutions while retaining the advantages of projection-based reduced dynamics, offering a promising framework for fast, physically grounded data-assisted simulation.

title: Direct-Write Chemical Vapor Deposition
summary: Direct-write pattering, using chemical vapor deposition through a nozzle, enables localized film growth using high-purity precursors standard to the electronics industry. Yet, achieving sub 100 $μ\mathrm{m}$ feature control has been limited by nozzle design and unquantified precursor surface diffusion. Here, we report a direct-write chemical vapor deposition platform that employs a 10 $μ\mathrm{m}$ tip diameter glass micro-nozzle mounted on a scanning stage above a heated substrate in ultra-high vacuum. Using this approach, we demonstrate the continuous single-pass writing of 500 $\mathrm{nm}$ thick metallic aluminum lines with a 30 $μ\mathrm{m}$ linewidth on titanium nitride-coated silicon. This capability enables maskless, localized growth under systematically varied deposition conditions on a single substrate. To analyze the resulting deposit profiles, we introduce a transport framework coupling Knudsen gas emission from the micro-nozzle with surface diffusion to extract the effective precursor diffusion length, $L_d$. $L_d$ captures the combined impact of precursor surface mobility, residence time, substrate temperature ($165^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $205^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), growth duration, and nozzle height, contracting from 17.4 $μ\mathrm{m}$ down to 3.2 $μ\mathrm{m}$ at elevated temperatures. These results establish $L_d$ as a quantitative parameter for evaluating laterally confined chemical vapor growth and predicting feature resolution limits. This approach provides a practical methodology to measure and quantify precursor surface transport in localized film synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a direct-write chemical vapor deposition (CVD) platform using a 10 μm glass micro-nozzle in UHV to write 500 nm-thick aluminum lines with 30 μm linewidth, and introduces a transport model coupling Knudsen emission with surface diffusion to extract an effective precursor diffusion length Ld.
AI.motivation: Direct-write CVD via nozzles enables localized film growth with high-purity precursors, but achieving sub-100 μm feature control has been hindered by nozzle design limitations and unquantified precursor surface diffusion.
AI.method: A 10 μm tip-diameter glass micro-nozzle on a scanning stage is positioned above a heated substrate in ultra-high vacuum, enabling continuous single-pass writing under systematically varied deposition conditions. Deposit profiles are analyzed with a transport framework coupling Knudsen gas emission from the micro-nozzle with surface diffusion.
AI.result: Continuous single-pass writing of 500 nm-thick metallic aluminum lines with 30 μm linewidth on titanium nitride-coated silicon is demonstrated. The extracted effective precursor diffusion length Ld contracts from 17.4 μm to 3.2 μm as substrate temperature rises from 165 °C to 205 °C, capturing the combined effects of precursor surface mobility, residence time, substrate temperature, growth duration, and nozzle height.
AI.conclusion: Ld is established as a quantitative parameter for evaluating laterally confined chemical vapor growth and predicting feature resolution limits, providing a practical methodology to measure and quantify precursor surface transport in localized film synthesis.

title: Replica Fragmentation and Glassy Dynamics in Parity Learning
summary: We study how independently trained Transformer neural networks reconstruct a binary string from its local domain walls. Runs sharing the data and training protocol can realize different functions. We treat them as replicas and measure truth alignment $m$, prediction confidence $q_{\mathrm{self}}$, and cross-replica agreement $q_{\mathrm{cross}}$. Confident disagreement defines the finite-size replica fragmentation that we call glass-like. With small training sets, replicas predict all training examples correctly but remain confident in incorrect predictions for unseen inputs, a regime we call memorization. With larger sets, runs can generalize and then retreat. Retreat occurs when outputs start to deviate from truth while confidence remains high. The frontier between learned and unlearned outputs recedes toward shorter strings. Many later recover as the frontier advances again. The self--cross gap $q_{\mathrm{self}}-q_{\mathrm{cross}}$ clearly distinguishes the three learning regimes of memorization, retreat, and recovery. With overall and position-dependent truth alignment subtracted, their residual correlations also differ: memorizing replicas have weakly and uniformly correlated residuals, while retreat has the largest fraction of replica pairs whose residuals are anti-correlated. That is, on the inputs where one replica of such a pair does better than its average, the other tends to do worse. These finite-size observations distinguish persistent memorization from ongoing retreat--recovery dynamics. The thermodynamic and long-time limits, and extensions to other learning tasks, remain open.

AI.tldr: Independently trained Transformers reconstructing a binary string from local domain walls exhibit three learning regimes—memorization, retreat, and recovery—distinguished by the self–cross confidence gap and residual correlation structure, revealing glass-like replica fragmentation.
AI.motivation: Independently trained neural networks can converge to different functions despite identical data and protocols, raising questions about the nature of these functional differences and how learning dynamics progress. This work aims to characterize these replica-like differences and identify signatures that distinguish distinct learning regimes.
AI.method: The authors train multiple Transformer networks to reconstruct a binary string from its local domain walls. They treat separately trained runs as replicas and measure truth alignment m, self-confidence q_self, and cross-replica agreement q_cross. They define glass-like replica fragmentation via confident disagreement and analyze the self–cross confidence gap and residual correlations (after subtracting overall and position-dependent truth alignment) across training set sizes.
AI.result: Small training sets yield memorization: replicas predict training examples correctly but are confidently wrong on unseen inputs. Larger sets enable generalization followed by retreat, where outputs deviate from truth while confidence stays high, with the learned/unlearned frontier receding toward shorter strings before many later recover. The self–cross gap q_self − q_cross cleanly separates memorization, retreat, and recovery. Residual correlations differ: memorizing replicas show weak, uniform correlations, whereas retreat has the largest fraction of anti-correlated replica pairs.
AI.conclusion: The self–cross gap and residual correlation structure provide clear signatures distinguishing persistent memorization from ongoing retreat–recovery dynamics. These finite-size observations characterize glass-like replica fragmentation. Thermodynamic and long-time limits, as well as extensions to other learning tasks, remain open.

title: Spatial density, first passage times, and entropy of run and tumble particles in a bistable potential
summary: We study the dynamics of a run and tumble particle (RTP) in a bistable potential, in contact with a heat bath. We find the exact form of the steady state position distribution as well as its time-dependent form in Laplace space. We use this result to study relaxation properties of the spatial probability density and find that it converges to the steady state from the center outwards, with the relaxation front moving ballistically in time. Physically this ballistic behavior arises when observing relaxation properties at the tails of the density, where the distance of the particle from the origin is larger than the length-scale describing the steady state of the RTP. We also find the exact form of the mean first passage time, and the long-time behavior of the first passage time distribution. This allows us to coarse-grain the dynamics as a dichotomous Markov process, a paradigm for a wide class of bistable processes. Coarse-graining, however, comes at the cost of a loss of information: while the RTP possesses a finite entropy production even at steady state, it identically vanishes for its coarse-grained description.

AI.tldr: The authors solve exactly the steady state and time-dependent (Laplace space) position distribution of a run-and-tumble particle in a bistable potential, showing ballistic relaxation from the center outwards, computing first passage statistics, and constructing a coarse-grained dichotomous Markov description that loses the steady-state entropy production.
AI.motivation: Run-and-tumble particles (RTPs) are a canonical model of active matter, but their behavior in bistable potentials—relevant to trapping, switching, and escape phenomena—is far less understood than in harmonic or free settings. A key open question is how active self-propulsion alters relaxation dynamics and thermodynamic costs (entropy production) relative to a passive bistable system, and whether a simplified coarse-grained description can faithfully capture these features.
AI.method: The authors analyze an RTP moving in a bistable potential while coupled to a thermal bath. They derive the exact steady-state position distribution and its time-dependent counterpart in Laplace space. From these they extract relaxation properties of the spatial probability density and identify the relaxation front dynamics. They also compute the exact mean first passage time and the long-time asymptotics of the first passage time distribution. These results are then used to coarse-grain the dynamics into a dichotomous Markov process.
AI.result: The steady-state position distribution is obtained exactly in closed form, along with its Laplace-space time-dependent form. The relaxation of the spatial density toward steady state proceeds from the center outwards, with the relaxation front moving ballistically in time; this ballistic behavior emerges when probing the tails, where the distance from the origin exceeds the length scale governing the RTP steady state. The exact mean first passage time and the long-time behavior of the first passage time distribution are derived. The coarse-grained dichotomous Markov process reproduces the bistable switching, but while the full RTP has finite entropy production even at steady state, the coarse-grained description yields identically zero entropy production.
AI.conclusion: The RTP in a bistable potential admits exact analytical treatment, revealing ballistic relaxation fronts, exact first passage statistics, and a coarse-graining to a dichotomous Markov process. This coarse-graining, although a paradigm for bistable processes, is lossy: it erases the steady-state entropy production that the full RTP exhibits, highlighting that thermodynamic irreversibility is not captured by reduced bistable descriptions.

title: Accurate Molecular Property Regression Using Simple Fusion of Complementary Classical and Graph Predictors
summary: Accurate prediction of continuous molecular properties supports chemical discovery and design. Many recent approaches combine multiple molecular representations within increasingly complex neural architectures, aiming to achieve higher accuracy. However, classical machine-learning models remain competitive when trained on chemically meaningful molecular representations. We therefore constructed a chemistry-guided classical branch from Morgan fingerprints, RDKit molecular descriptors, and conformer-derived geometric features selected to provide complementary views of molecular structure. We combined four tree learners trained on these representations with a CoMPT graph predictor and integrated their out-of-fold predictions using Ridge regression. Across ESOL, FreeSolv, and Lipophilicity datasets, the fused model achieved lower mean root-mean-square error (RMSE) than Chemprop and competitive graph and multimodal methods, including CoMPT, MoleSG, KFLM2, and MCMPP. After retraining on the separately curated AqSolDB dataset, the same approach, without redesign or retuning, reduced mean absolute error (MAE) relative to the classical ensemble and achieved lower mean MAE than Chemprop. These results show that accurate and transferable molecular property regression does not necessarily require a complex joint multimodal architecture: classical learning remains competitive when chemical insight guides the choice of molecular representations, and a graph model can add complementary information through simple prediction-level fusion.

AI.tldr: A chemistry-guided classical ensemble (Morgan fingerprints, RDKit descriptors, conformer geometric features with tree learners) fused at prediction level with a CoMPT graph predictor via Ridge regression matches or beats complex multimodal architectures on molecular property regression, indicating that chemical insight in representation choice matters more than architectural complexity.
AI.motivation: Many recent molecular property prediction approaches combine multiple molecular representations within increasingly complex neural architectures to chase higher accuracy. Yet classical machine-learning models trained on chemically meaningful representations remain competitive, suggesting that the added complexity of joint multimodal architectures may not be necessary for accurate and transferable regression.
AI.method: A chemistry-guided classical branch was built from Morgan fingerprints, RDKit molecular descriptors, and conformer-derived geometric features chosen to provide complementary views of molecular structure. Four tree learners trained on these representations were combined with a CoMPT graph predictor, and their out-of-fold predictions were integrated using Ridge regression (prediction-level fusion).
AI.result: Across ESOL, FreeSolv, and Lipophilicity, the fused model achieved lower mean RMSE than Chemprop and was competitive with graph and multimodal methods including CoMPT, MoleSG, KFLM2, and MCMPP. After retraining on the separately curated AqSolDB dataset without redesign or retuning, the same approach reduced MAE relative to the classical ensemble and achieved lower mean MAE than Chemprop.
AI.conclusion: Accurate and transferable molecular property regression does not necessarily require a complex joint multimodal architecture. Classical learning remains competitive when chemical insight guides the choice of molecular representations, and a graph model can contribute complementary information through simple prediction-level fusion.

title: Theory of Magic Angles in Twisted Bilayer Graphene: from Non-Abelian Gauge Fields to Flat Bands
summary: At a discrete set of ``magic'' twist angles, twisted bilayer graphene develops two bands at charge neutrality that are almost perfectly flat. We present a unified theory of this phenomenon within the chiral continuum model. The central object is the square of the chiral Hamiltonian, a $2\times2$ Schrödinger operator for an electron moving in a non-Abelian $SU(2)$ pseudo-magnetic field generated by the interlayer tunneling. From it we derive an energy sum rule in which the interlayer coupling splits into a bounded overlap channel and an unbounded current channel; their different scaling with the coupling $α$ explains why the first magic angle is qualitatively different from the rest. The asymptotic rule $α_{m+1}-α_m\to3/2$ follows from a rescaling of the moiré potential together with its three-cell magnetic periodicity, with the two parity families of zero modes each repeating with period $3$ and interleaved with each other. Near the AA point the zero-mode problem becomes a lowest-Landau-level problem in an effective field $B_{\rm eff}=3α$, so that the high-order zero modes are coherent Landau states of width $1/\sqrt{3α}$ whose guiding centres converge to $\pm(π/3) q_μ$, with kinetic and confinement energies in equipartition. Deforming the coupling into an Abelian one removes the magic-angle sequence, which shows that the non-Abelian structure is essential. Between consecutive magic angles, band inversions at $Γ$ and $M$ produce phases with Chern numbers $C=\pm2$, and the quantum metric reaches a sharp maximum at $θ\approx0.43^\circ$, identifying a promising regime for correlated and topological phases beyond the first magic angle.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified theory of magic-angle flat bands in the chiral continuum model of twisted bilayer graphene, deriving them from the squared chiral Hamiltonian as a Schrödinger operator in a non-Abelian SU(2) pseudo-magnetic field, explaining the energy sum rule, the asymptotic magic-angle spacing, high-order zero-mode structure, and the emergence of Chern phases and a quantum-metric maximum.
AI.motivation: Twisted bilayer graphene hosts nearly flat bands at magic angles, but a unified understanding of why these angles arise and why the first magic angle differs qualitatively from the rest has been lacking.
AI.method: The authors work within the chiral continuum model, using the square of the chiral Hamiltonian—a 2x2 Schrödinger operator in a non-Abelian SU(2) pseudo-magnetic field from interlayer tunneling—to derive an energy sum rule separating interlayer coupling into bounded overlap and unbounded current channels.
AI.result: They obtain the asymptotic rule α_{m+1}-α_m→3/2, show two parity families of zero modes repeat with period 3 and interleave, reduce the zero-mode problem near AA to a lowest-Landau-level problem with B_eff=3α and coherent Landau states of width 1/√(3α), find magic angles vanish for Abelian coupling, and identify Chern numbers C=±2 phases between magic angles plus a sharp quantum-metric maximum at θ≈0.43°.
AI.conclusion: Magic-angle flat bands arise from the non-Abelian structure of the interlayer coupling, with the first magic angle being qualitatively distinct due to the different scaling of overlap and current channels; the theory unifies the sequence's asymptotics, zero-mode structure, and topological/correlated regimes beyond the first magic angle.

title: Odd-parity magnon spin polarization from chiral four-spin exchange in a honeycomb antiferromagnet
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, plus 6 pages of Supplemental Material
summary: Chiral four-spin exchange generates a momentum-dependent magnon spin in a compensated honeycomb antiferromagnet at zero magnetic field. For a Néel vector tilted by an angle $θ_0$ from the layer normal, the interaction contributes to intersublattice magnon pairing already at harmonic order, with an amplitude proportional to $\cosθ_0\sin^2θ_0$. Biaxial anisotropy mixes the two longitudinal-spin sectors, producing nonquantized mode spins that are odd in momentum, while a sublattice-exchange relation keeps the magnon energies reciprocal. A temperature gradient then induces a spin density along the Néel axis through a redistribution of magnon occupations. Reversing the four-spin coupling reverses this spin density and the mode spins without changing the magnon energies. MnPS$_3$ motivates the magnetic geometry; realizing the interaction requires a structural modification compatible with the symmetry assumptions of the model.

AI.tldr: Chiral four-spin exchange in a compensated honeycomb antiferromagnet generates momentum-dependent, nonquantized magnon spin at zero field, enabling a temperature-gradient-induced spin density along the Néel axis that reverses with the sign of the four-spin coupling while magnon energies remain reciprocal and unchanged.
AI.motivation: Conventional magnon spin transport typically requires magnetic fields or noncollinear spin textures. The paper seeks a zero-field mechanism for generating momentum-dependent magnon spin in a compensated collinear antiferromagnet, motivated by the magnetic geometry of MnPS3.
AI.method: The authors analyze a Néel vector tilted by θ0 from the layer normal in a compensated honeycomb antiferromagnet. Chiral four-spin exchange at harmonic order produces intersublattice magnon pairing with amplitude ∝ cosθ0 sin²θ0. Biaxial anisotropy mixes the two longitudinal-spin sectors, yielding mode spins odd in momentum while a sublattice-exchange relation enforces reciprocal magnon energies. A temperature gradient drives magnon occupation redistribution.
AI.result: The interaction generates momentum-dependent magnon spin even with zero magnetic field. The resulting mode spins are nonquantized and odd in momentum. A temperature gradient induces a spin density along the Néel axis. Reversing the four-spin coupling reverses both the spin density and the mode spins, but leaves the magnon energies unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Chiral four-spin exchange provides a route to zero-field, momentum-dependent magnon spin and thermally induced spin density in compensated honeycomb antiferromagnets, with MnPS3 as a motivating geometry; however, realizing the required interaction demands a structural modification consistent with the model's symmetry assumptions.

title: Effect of Source-to-Substrate Distance on the Optical and Electrical Properties of Thermally Deposited CdTe, CdSe and Sb$_2$S$_3$ Thin Films
summary: In this work, cadmium telluride (CdTe), cadmium selenide (CdSe), and antimony sulfide (Sb\(_2\)S\(_3\)) thin films were deposited using the thermal evaporation technique by varying the source-to-substrate distance (SSD) from 15 to 24 cm (15, 18, 21, and 24 cm). The influence of the SSD on the structural, compositional, optical and electrical properties of the deposited films was systematically investigated. XRD analysis revealed the polycrystalline nature of the CdTe and CdSe thin films, whereas the Sb$_2$S$_3$ thin films exhibited an amorphous nature. EDX spectroscopy confirmed the presence of the constituent elements in the deposited films. Optical analysis revealed a marginal variation in the optical band gap with increasing SSD, while the film thickness, determined using the envelope method, decreased with increasing SSD. The optical band gap energies of CdTe and CdSe were found to be below 2 eV, whereas Sb$_2$S$_3$ exhibited a relatively higher band gap. The relatively low band gap energies and high absorption coefficients of the CdTe and CdSe films make them promising candidates for absorber layer applications in thin film solar cells (TFSCs). The films exhibited relatively low optical transmittance, which is desirable for efficient light absorption in absorber layers. Electrical characterization confirmed the semiconducting nature of all the deposited thin films. Overall, the results demonstrate that the optical and electrical properties of CdTe, CdSe and Sb$_2$S$_3$ thin films can be effectively modified by varying the SSD. The findings indicate that, in addition to the well established CdTe absorber, CdSe thin films show potential for application as absorber materials in TFSCs.

AI.tldr: CdTe, CdSe, and Sb2S3 thin films were deposited by thermal evaporation at varying source-to-substrate distances (15–24 cm), and the effects on structural, compositional, optical, and electrical properties were systematically studied to evaluate their suitability as absorber layers in thin film solar cells.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to tune and understand how deposition geometry—specifically source-to-substrate distance (SSD)—affects the properties of CdTe, CdSe, and Sb2S3 thin films, in order to identify promising absorber materials for thin film solar cells (TFSCs).
AI.method: Thin films of CdTe, CdSe, and Sb2S3 were deposited via thermal evaporation with SSD varied from 15 to 24 cm (15, 18, 21, 24 cm). Structural and compositional properties were characterized by XRD and EDX. Optical properties (band gap, thickness via envelope method, transmittance, absorption coefficient) and electrical properties were also measured and correlated with SSD.
AI.result: XRD showed CdTe and CdSe films are polycrystalline, while Sb2S3 films are amorphous. EDX confirmed constituent elements. Film thickness decreased with increasing SSD, while the optical band gap showed only marginal variation. CdTe and CdSe had band gaps below 2 eV with high absorption coefficients; Sb2S3 had a relatively higher band gap. All films showed low optical transmittance, and electrical characterization confirmed semiconducting behavior.
AI.conclusion: Varying SSD effectively modifies the optical and electrical properties of CdTe, CdSe, and Sb2S3 thin films. Low band gaps and high absorption coefficients of CdTe and CdSe make them promising absorber layer candidates for TFSCs. Besides the established CdTe absorber, CdSe thin films also show potential as absorber materials in TFSCs.

title: Fast free-energy estimation for complex systems with nonreversible simulated tempering
summary: We discuss free-energy estimation for complex systems using simulated tempering with Wang--Landau-type feedback. We show that introducing nonreversible dynamics in temperature space and multiple temperature updates per step significantly accelerates the convergence of the free-energy estimate. We then apply the algorithm to the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson spin-glass model. Our results show that the algorithm can precisely estimate the free energy up to a large system size $L \simeq 64$, and that subsequent equilibrium simulated tempering simulations with the estimated free energy can rapidly sample from the Boltzmann distributions over a wide temperature range that covers the spin-glass transition temperature. The convergence time of our algorithm grows much more slowly with system size than that of another known algorithm for on-the-fly free-energy estimation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a free-energy estimation method combining simulated tempering with Wang-Landau-type feedback, using nonreversible temperature dynamics and multiple updates per step to accelerate convergence, and validates it on the 3D Edwards-Anderson spin-glass model up to system size L≈64.
AI.motivation: Estimating free energy for complex systems such as spin glasses is challenging because convergence of on-the-fly free-energy estimation is slow, especially as system size grows, limiting the ability to sample Boltzmann distributions over wide temperature ranges.
AI.method: The authors use simulated tempering with Wang-Landau-type feedback for free-energy estimation. They introduce nonreversible dynamics in temperature space and perform multiple temperature updates per step to significantly accelerate convergence of the free-energy estimate.
AI.result: Applied to the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson spin-glass model, the algorithm precisely estimates free energy up to large system size L≈64. Subsequent equilibrium simulated tempering simulations using the estimated free energy rapidly sample Boltzmann distributions over a wide temperature range covering the spin-glass transition temperature. Convergence time grows much more slowly with system size than that of another known on-the-fly free-energy estimation algorithm.
AI.conclusion: The proposed simulated tempering scheme with Wang-Landau-type feedback provides an efficient and precise approach for free-energy estimation in complex systems, enabling rapid equilibrium sampling over broad temperature ranges and scaling better with system size than existing methods.

title: Closed analytical form of many-body free volume and thermodynamics of monodisperse hard disks
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, to be published in J. Chem. Phys
summary: The hard disk model is a fundamental reference system for excluded volume physics, liquid structure, and 2D ordering. Yet, despite its apparent simplicity, an analytical formulation of its thermodynamics has remained difficult because the free volume available to disks centers has a highly nontrivial many-body geometry. Here we show that this geometry admits a closed and exact representation: for any given hard disk configuration, the free volume can be analytically expressed through intersection areas of up to five exclusion disks. This provides a direct geometrical route from particle coordinates to the configurational partition function and entropy. We prove that the N disk partition function factorizes into a product of conditional free volumes and identify its two limiting asymptotic forms: the low density fluid regime controlled by extensive cavities and the high density fluid regime controlled by intensive private cells. Using the geometric measures computed from representative equilibrium particle configurations, the resulting theory reproduces the established hard disk equation of state over almost the entire density range up to close packing. At intermediate densities, the analysis reveals a mixed fluid regime in which localized caged defects provide an additional configurational entropy within the density interval preceding liquid hexatic coexistence. Finally, the five disk intersection area is shown to be a sensitive local scalar measure of hexagonal ordering, complementing the orientational order parameter and emphasizing the central role of many-body correlations.

AI.tldr: The free volume of hard disks admits a closed exact representation via intersection areas of up to five exclusion disks, enabling an analytic route from particle coordinates to the partition function, entropy, and an accurate equation of state.
AI.motivation: The hard disk model is a fundamental reference system for excluded volume physics, liquid structure, and 2D ordering, but despite its apparent simplicity an analytical formulation of its thermodynamics has remained difficult because the free volume available to disk centers has a highly nontrivial many-body geometry.
AI.method: The authors derive a closed, exact geometric representation of the free volume: for any hard disk configuration, the free volume is analytically expressed through intersection areas of up to five exclusion disks, giving a direct geometrical route from particle coordinates to the configurational partition function and entropy. They prove that the N-disk partition function factorizes into a product of conditional free volumes and identify two limiting asymptotic forms—a low density fluid regime controlled by extensive cavities and a high density fluid regime controlled by intensive private cells. Geometric measures are computed from representative equilibrium particle configurations to construct the theory.
AI.result: The resulting theory reproduces the established hard disk equation of state over almost the entire density range up to close packing. At intermediate densities, the analysis reveals a mixed fluid regime in which localized caged defects provide additional configurational entropy within the density interval preceding liquid-hexatic coexistence. The five disk intersection area is shown to be a sensitive local scalar measure of hexagonal ordering, complementing the orientational order parameter.
AI.conclusion: Free volume geometry can be cast in an exact closed form based on intersections of up to five exclusion disks, yielding a factorized partition function and a quantitatively accurate hard disk equation of state. This highlights the central role of many-body correlations and provides a local scalar diagnostic of hexagonal ordering alongside the orientational order parameter.

title: Learning consistent molecular mechanics force fields from first principles
comment: Accepted to the ML4Molecules Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Classical force fields (FFs) remain the workhorse for large-scale simulations even as machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach ab initio accuracy. They decompose total configuration energies into simple effective interactions whose parameters are traditionally assigned based on atom or bond types, enabling efficient simulations but also limiting their ability to adapt across configurations. Recent machine learning approaches have improved the accuracy and transferability of bonded parameters in these FFs by inferring them as functions of local atomic environments, but still rely on empirical nonbonded parameters for practical simulations. In this work, we introduce a unified approach, \texttt{grappa-fullFF}, which learns both bonded and nonbonded parameters \emph{consistently} and simultaneously from ab initio reference data. By incorporating physically inspired regularization via supervision of the electrostatic potential and an architecture that facilitates charge equilibration, our model recovers accurate electric response properties, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on geometry optimization benchmarks, and reproduces the conformational sampling of both classical and existing machine-learned FFs, without relying on externally assigned nonbonded parameters.

AI.tldr: grappa-fullFF learns bonded and nonbonded force-field parameters consistently and simultaneously from ab initio data using electrostatic-potential regularization and charge equilibration, matching state-of-the-art geometry optimization and conformational sampling without externally assigned nonbonded parameters.
AI.motivation: Classical force fields are efficient for large-scale simulation but rely on type-based parameters that limit adaptability, while recent ML approaches improve only bonded parameters and still depend on empirical nonbonded parameters, leaving a gap for a fully learned, physically consistent force field.
AI.method: A unified model (grappa-fullFF) that learns bonded and nonbonded parameters consistently and simultaneously from ab initio reference data, incorporating physically inspired regularization via supervision of the electrostatic potential and an architecture enabling charge equilibration.
AI.result: Recovers accurate electric response properties, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on geometry optimization benchmarks, and reproduces the conformational sampling of both classical and existing machine-learned force fields, without relying on externally assigned nonbonded parameters.
AI.conclusion: Consistently learning bonded and nonbonded terms from ab initio data yields an accurate, transferable force field that matches classical and machine-learned baselines in sampling and optimization without empirical nonbonded inputs.

title: Ferroaxial Electronic Response to Local Lattice Rotation
summary: We theoretically investigate electronic responses to lattice deformation in a ferroaxial system using a tight-binding model on a two-dimensional square lattice and linear response theory. While conventional elastic responses are commonly discussed in terms of symmetric strain, the displacement gradient also contains an antisymmetric component describing a local lattice rotation. Focusing on this rotational degree of freedom, we treat the symmetric strain and antisymmetric local rotation as independent perturbations and incorporate their effects microscopically through deformation-induced modulations of the electronic hopping amplitudes. We find that the local rotation induces characteristic diagonal electric quadrupoles that are distinct from those generated by the symmetric shear strain. The rotation-induced response is dominated by the intraband contribution and increases approximately linearly with the ferroaxial crystal field, vanishing in the absence of ferroaxial order. In contrast, the symmetric-shear-induced response remains finite without ferroaxial order and contains both intraband and interband contributions. These results demonstrate that the antisymmetric local rotation provides a distinct electronic response channel characteristic of the ferroaxial state.

AI.tldr: This work theoretically shows that antisymmetric local lattice rotation, treated as an independent perturbation from symmetric strain, drives a distinct electric-quadrupole electronic response that is characteristic of the ferroaxial state in a 2D tight-binding model.
AI.motivation: Conventional elastic responses are usually discussed only via symmetric strain, while the displacement gradient also contains an antisymmetric component describing local lattice rotation. The authors aim to isolate this rotational degree of freedom and clarify whether it produces a distinct electronic response tied to ferroaxial order.
AI.method: A tight-binding model on a two-dimensional square lattice combined with linear response theory. Symmetric strain and antisymmetric local rotation are treated as independent perturbations, entering microscopically as deformation-induced modulations of the electronic hopping amplitudes.
AI.result: Local rotation induces diagonal electric quadrupoles distinct from those from symmetric shear strain. The rotation-induced response is dominated by intraband contributions, grows approximately linearly with the ferroaxial crystal field, and vanishes without ferroaxial order. The symmetric-shear-induced response remains finite without ferroaxial order and contains both intraband and interband contributions.
AI.conclusion: Antisymmetric local rotation provides a distinct electronic response channel that is characteristic of the ferroaxial state, distinguishing it from conventional symmetric-strain responses.

title: Two-exciton bound states in the Merrifield exciton model
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, to appear in Phys. Rev. B
summary: Understanding the formation and dynamics of two-exciton bound states (BSs) is crucial for harnessing multi-exciton phenomena and designing next-generation organic semiconductor materials. While various mechanisms such as intermolecular exciton-exciton interactions or multi-level intramolecular configurations can generate these BSs, a fundamental understanding of their underlying lattice dynamics remains a key challenge. Within this context, the Merrifield exciton model stands out as a premier framework for capturing the intricate quantum mixing between single-site doubly-excited states and two-particle scattering continuum. In this work, by constructing a set of exact two-exciton Bloch states and applying a plane-wave ansatz to treat the resulting inhomogeneous tridiagonal matrices, we provide a complete, rigorous solution to the two-exciton problem in a finite-size Merrifield chain. We analytically map the parameter regions that support two-exciton BSs, proving that at most two distinct types of BSs can emerge, located either above or below the scattering continuum. Furthermore, we provide a quantitative interpretation of how these two types of BSs evolve as a function of the total wave number within the whole Brillouin zone. The obtained closed-form expressions for the eigenenergies and wave functions offer valuable benchmarks for exploring exciton dynamics and optical responses in related molecular aggregates.

AI.tldr: This work provides an exact, rigorous solution to the two-exciton problem in a finite-size Merrifield chain by constructing exact two-exciton Bloch states, analytically mapping the parameter regions for two-exciton bound states and showing that at most two types of BSs can emerge above or below the scattering continuum.
AI.motivation: Understanding two-exciton bound-state formation and dynamics is essential for multi-exciton phenomena and organic semiconductor design, yet the underlying lattice dynamics remain poorly understood, motivating a rigorous treatment of the Merrifield exciton model.
AI.method: The authors construct a set of exact two-exciton Bloch states and apply a plane-wave ansatz to handle the resulting inhomogeneous tridiagonal matrices, yielding a complete analytical solution for the two-exciton problem in a finite-size Merrifield chain.
AI.result: Analytical mapping of parameter regions supporting two-exciton BSs proves at most two distinct types of BSs can emerge, located either above or below the scattering continuum, and quantitatively describes their evolution with the total wave number across the entire Brillouin zone.
AI.conclusion: The closed-form expressions for eigenenergies and wave functions provide valuable benchmarks for studying exciton dynamics and optical responses in related molecular aggregates.

title: Conditions for Altermagnetism in RuO2
summary: The magnetic ground state of rutile RuO2 remains disputed, raising a central question: under what structural and chemical conditions can this material support altermagnetism? We address this question by combining a critical assessment of experimental and theoretical studies with first-principles calculations of epitaxial strain, point defects, doping, and interfaces. Bulk-sensitive measurements reported in the literature are consistent with a nonmagnetic ground state, while magnetic signatures in thin films depend strongly on their structural environment and do not necessarily establish homogeneous altermagnetic order. Our calculations identify substrate-imposed epitaxial strain as the leading factor favoring altermagnetism among the conditions examined and predict several substrate-orientation combinations that stabilize an altermagnetic ground state. Carrier doping and chemical substitution modify this strain-induced magnetism in distinct ways. Uniform hole doping strengthens the magnetic tendency, whereas Ru vacancies provide little benefit and can weaken the magnetic state through local structural distortions. Cr or Mn substitution, by contrast, enhances Ru magnetic moments and further stabilizes the strained altermagnetic phase. These results distinguish the effects of carrier doping from those of local structural and chemical changes and identify concrete routes to realizing altermagnetism in RuO2 films.

AI.tldr: Bulk RuO2 is nonmagnetic, but substrate-imposed epitaxial strain is identified as the dominant factor that can stabilize altermagnetism in RuO2 films, with hole doping and Cr/Mn substitution further enhancing it.
AI.motivation: The magnetic ground state of rutile RuO2 is disputed. A central open question is under what structural and chemical conditions this material can support altermagnetism, motivating a systematic reconciliation of experiment and theory.
AI.method: Critical assessment of existing experimental and theoretical literature combined with first-principles calculations examining epitaxial strain, point defects, carrier doping, chemical substitution, and interfaces.
AI.result: Bulk-sensitive measurements are consistent with a nonmagnetic ground state, while thin-film magnetic signatures are strongly environment-dependent and do not necessarily prove homogeneous altermagnetic order. Epitaxial strain emerges as the leading factor favoring altermagnetism, with several substrate-orientation combinations predicted to stabilize an altermagnetic ground state. Hole doping strengthens the magnetic tendency, Ru vacancies offer little benefit and can weaken magnetism via local structural distortions, and Cr or Mn substitution enhances Ru moments and further stabilizes the strained altermagnetic phase.
AI.conclusion: The work distinguishes carrier-doping effects from local structural and chemical effects and identifies concrete routes—chiefly strain engineering, complemented by hole doping and Cr/Mn substitution—to realize altermagnetism in RuO2 films.

title: Hamiltonian curl-forces in systems coupled to multiple thermal reservoirs
summary: We investigate the statistical mechanics of a system coupled to multiple heat reservoirs at different temperatures, a setting which typically sustains nontrivial circulation. By applying a canonical transformation, we map the system onto that of a particle coupled to a single reservoir yet driven by a deterministic curl-force---a reversible, velocity-independent non-conservative force with non-vanishing curl---that can be described by a Hamiltonian with an anisotropic kinetic energy term. Despite the Hamiltonian structure, the system does not relax to the corresponding Boltzmann distribution, and is genuinely out of equilibrium. The mapping provides a mechanical interpretation of the currents in multi-temperature systems, as we demonstrate by means of two examples. In particular, the direction of circulation is qualitatively predictable from the deterministic force field. For the exactly solvable case of an $N$-dimensional underdamped Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, we derive explicit expressions for the steady-state distribution and the entropy production rate, highlighting the role of the (generalized) curl of the force field in driving the system out of thermal equilibrium. Finally, we show how a non-conservative force can be used to exactly equilibrate any system coupled to multiple reservoirs, and obtain the corresponding equilibrium distribution.

AI.tldr: A multi-temperature system is mapped, via a canonical transformation, onto a single-reservoir particle driven by a deterministic curl-force, revealing a mechanical interpretation of non-equilibrium currents and yielding exact steady-state and entropy-production results for an N-dimensional underdamped Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.
AI.motivation: Systems coupled to multiple heat reservoirs at different temperatures typically sustain nontrivial circulation and are genuinely out of equilibrium, yet a mechanical understanding of their currents is lacking. The paper seeks a mechanical interpretation of these currents and a framework for controlling non-equilibrium behavior.
AI.method: A canonical transformation maps the multi-reservoir system onto a particle coupled to a single reservoir but driven by a reversible, velocity-independent non-conservative curl-force (non-vanishing curl), expressible via a Hamiltonian with anisotropic kinetic energy. Two examples illustrate circulation predictability from the deterministic force field, and the N-dimensional underdamped Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is solved exactly for the steady-state distribution and entropy production rate.
AI.result: Steady-state distribution and entropy production rate are derived explicitly for the N-dimensional underdamped Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; the generalized curl of the force field is shown to drive the system out of thermal equilibrium. The circulation direction is qualitatively predictable from the deterministic force field. A non-conservative force can exactly equilibrate any system coupled to multiple reservoirs, giving the corresponding equilibrium distribution.
AI.conclusion: Despite possessing a Hamiltonian structure, the mapped system does not relax to the corresponding Boltzmann distribution and is genuinely out of equilibrium. The mapping offers a mechanical interpretation of currents in multi-temperature systems and demonstrates that tailored non-conservative forces can exactly equilibrate multi-reservoir systems.

title: Negative charging energy in LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ quantum dots induced by SrTiO$_3$ polarization
summary: We propose a microscopic mechanism for the negative charging energy in LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ quantum dots, arising from the electrostatic image charge associated with the paraelectric response of SrTiO$_3$. Using a self-consistent configuration-interaction approach that accounts for both Coulomb repulsion and image-charge interactions, we find a robust regime of electron pairing whose strength is tunable through the confinement potential and the effective image-charge distance, set by the thickness of the interfacial two-dimensional electron gas. Our results establish dielectric image-charge effects as a route to controllable electron pairing in oxide quantum dots and other materials with a strong dielectric response.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that the negative charging energy in LaAlO3/SrTiO3 quantum dots originates from electrostatic image charges tied to SrTiO3's paraelectric response, and shows this yields tunable electron pairing.
AI.motivation: The negative charging energy observed in LaAlO3/SrTiO3 quantum dots requires a microscopic explanation, and the role of SrTiO3's strong dielectric (paraelectric) response has not been captured mechanistically.
AI.method: A self-consistent configuration-interaction approach that simultaneously accounts for Coulomb repulsion and image-charge interactions associated with the paraelectric response of SrTiO3.
AI.result: A robust regime of electron pairing is found, whose strength is tunable via the confinement potential and the effective image-charge distance, the latter set by the thickness of the interfacial two-dimensional electron gas.
AI.conclusion: Dielectric image-charge effects constitute a viable route to controllable electron pairing in oxide quantum dots and in other materials exhibiting a strong dielectric response.

title: Gradual Localization of Itinerant Cobalt 3d Electrons in the Pyrochlore Ferromagnetic Metal LuInCo4
summary: We investigated the microscopic magnetic state of the itinerant-electron ferromagnet LuInCo4 with a cobalt pyrochlore lattice by means of powder and single-crystal neutron diffraction measurements. The powder neutron diffraction profiles at zero field are well described by a simple q = 0 collinear ferromagnetic structure with an ordered Co moment of 0.9 uB. Single-crystal neutron diffraction experiments further suggest the absence of both antiferromagnetic order and long-period helical magnetic modulation. In addition, diffuse magnetic scattering was observed around q = 0, with its intensity distribution gradually broadened in reciprocal space upon cooling. Based on these observations, we propose a possible microscopic origin of the low-temperature metamagnetic transition in terms of a ferromagnetic instability enhanced by gradual localization of the itinerant Co-3d electrons. These results suggest that LuInCo4 provides a model system for investigating the interplay between electron localization and itinerant-electron ferromagnetism in cobalt-based metallic pyrochlore compounds.

AI.tldr: Neutron diffraction on the itinerant ferromagnet LuInCo4 (Co pyrochlore lattice) reveals a simple q=0 collinear ferromagnetic ground state with 0.9 μB ordered Co moment, no antiferromagnetic or helical order, and diffuse magnetic scattering that broadens upon cooling, suggesting an itinerant ferromagnetic instability tied to progressive Co-3d localization.
AI.motivation: The low-temperature metamagnetic transition in LuInCo4 and the interplay between electron localization and itinerant-electron ferromagnetism in Co-based metallic pyrochlore compounds are not well understood, motivating a microscopic determination of its magnetic ground state.
AI.method: Powder and single-crystal neutron diffraction measurements were performed on LuInCo4 at zero field; the powder profiles were fitted to candidate magnetic structures, single-crystal experiments tested for antiferromagnetic order and long-period helical modulation, and the diffuse magnetic scattering around q=0 was analyzed via its reciprocal-space intensity distribution as a function of temperature.
AI.result: Powder profiles are well described by a simple q=0 collinear ferromagnetic structure with an ordered Co moment of 0.9 μB. Single-crystal diffraction indicates the absence of both antiferromagnetic order and long-period helical magnetic modulation. Diffuse magnetic scattering is observed around q=0, with its intensity distribution gradually broadening in reciprocal space upon cooling.
AI.conclusion: The observations point to a ferromagnetic instability enhanced by gradual localization of itinerant Co-3d electrons as a possible microscopic origin of the low-temperature metamagnetic transition. LuInCo4 is proposed as a model system for studying the interplay between electron localization and itinerant-electron ferromagnetism in cobalt-based metallic pyrochlore compounds.

title: Reliability of AI/ML Computational Searches for Magnetic Materials: Databases, Validation, and Synthesizability
summary: The rapid growth of AI/ML methods for materials discovery has increased the importance of the quality, physical completeness, and information content of computational databases. We examine these issues for magnetic materials, where incomplete sampling of competing magnetic states, chemical disorder, and finite-temperature properties can lead to apparently accurate but physically unreliable predictions. We propose a hierarchical discovery workflow combining independent ML models with explicit electronic-structure, magnetic, dynamical, thermodynamic, kinetic, and experimental validation. To incorporate kinetic accessibility into high-throughput screening, we introduce a dimensionless synthesis-window descriptor based on the relation between the chemical order-disorder and Tammann temperatures. A cluster-expansion analysis of Fe-Co-B illustrates the importance of this criterion: although ordered Fe3CoB2 is energetically favored at T=0, its small ordering energy produces an order-disorder temperature far below room temperature, making long-range Fe/Co ordering kinetically unachievable. These results demonstrate that reliable AI/ML discovery of magnetic materials requires databases and validation procedures that contain physical information relevant to the target functionality, rather than simply larger numbers of calculated structures.

AI.tldr: Reliable AI/ML-driven magnetic materials discovery demands physically complete databases and validation, not merely more computed structures; a hierarchical workflow with a synthesis-window descriptor captures kinetic accessibility.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of AI/ML methods for materials discovery has increased the importance of the quality, physical completeness, and information content of computational databases. For magnetic materials, incomplete sampling of competing magnetic states, chemical disorder, and finite-temperature properties can lead to apparently accurate but physically unreliable predictions.
AI.method: A hierarchical discovery workflow combining independent ML models with explicit validation across electronic-structure, magnetic, dynamical, thermodynamic, kinetic, and experimental levels. To incorporate kinetic accessibility into high-throughput screening, a dimensionless synthesis-window descriptor is introduced based on the relation between the chemical order-disorder temperature and the Tammann temperature. A cluster-expansion analysis of Fe-Co-B is used to test the criterion.
AI.result: In Fe-Co-B, ordered Fe3CoB2 is energetically favored at T=0, but its small ordering energy produces an order-disorder temperature far below room temperature, making long-range Fe/Co ordering kinetically unachievable.
AI.conclusion: Reliable AI/ML discovery of magnetic materials requires databases and validation procedures containing physical information relevant to the target functionality rather than simply larger numbers of calculated structures.

title: Calculation of structural symmetry and applicability of small AkBlCm nanoclusters (A=Rb, Cs; B=Pb, Sn, Bi; C=Cl, Br, I) as building blocks for synthesis of larger-size nanoclusters
summary: In this report we analyze charasteristics of structural symmetry of small AkBlCm nanoclusters (A - Rb, Cs; B - Pb, Sn, Bi; C - Cl, Br, I), binding energies, stability, and, ultimately, applicability as building blocks for construction of larger-size nanoclusters. Preliminary spatial modeling of ternary compound nanoclusters has been carried out on the basics of geometrical approach, namely interatomic distances taken as a sums of corresponding ionic radii. The geometry optimization and binding energies of the modeled structures have been determined through quantum-chemical calculations. Geometry optimization has been performed with Gaussian09 software package using Density Functional Theory (DFT) within the generalized gradient approximation of the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) and hybrid approximation of the Becke-3-Lee-Yang-Parr (B3LYP) exchange-correlation functionals. The Stuttgart/Dresden (SDD) and Los Alamos National Laboratory 2 Double Zeta (LANL2DZ) scalar-relativistic effective basic potentials were employed throughout the calculations. As a result of these calculations, a clear relationship between the atomic radii, their ratios within the nanoclusters and their stability has been obtained and analyzed.

AI.tldr: This study computationally models small ternary AkBlCm nanoclusters (A = Rb, Cs; B = Pb, Sn, Bi; C = Cl, Br, I), analyzing their structural symmetry, binding energies, and stability, and assessing their potential as building blocks for larger nanoclusters.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand the structural symmetry, stability, and binding energetics of small ternary compound nanoclusters, and evaluate whether they can serve as building blocks for constructing larger-size nanoclusters.
AI.method: Preliminary spatial modeling was performed using a geometrical approach, with interatomic distances set as sums of corresponding ionic radii. Geometry optimization and binding energy calculations were done via quantum-chemical calculations using the Gaussian09 package with DFT, employing PBE (GGA) and B3LYP (hybrid) exchange-correlation functionals, and SDD and LANL2DZ scalar-relativistic effective core potentials.
AI.result: A clear relationship was obtained and analyzed between atomic radii, their ratios within the nanoclusters, and the clusters' stability.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a correlation linking atomic radii and their intra-cluster ratios to the stability of small ternary nanoclusters, indicating their potential applicability as building blocks for larger nanoclusters.

title: Symmetry protected quantum many body scars through half-gauging
summary: We study the interplay between symmetry defects insertion and the phenomena of quantum many body scarring. We exploit a class of models obtained from an embedding mechanism that defines a stochastic matrix form hamiltonian, hosting zero energy many body scarred states. Such models display an interesting playground to explore the consequences of dualities, half-gauging operations and so on. We first show that inside this class of models, what are the conditions to still have scared states after defect insertion. The main result of our work is a detailed analysis of half-gauging in such chains, which introduces a non-trivial interface in our system, leading to scarred states protected by the underlying symmetries. The conclusions for half-gauged scarred systems are general and may lead to fruitful directions for higher dimension scarred physics and their robustness.

AI.tldr: This work investigates how inserting symmetry defects and performing half-gauging operations affect quantum many-body scarred states in a class of stochastic-matrix-form Hamiltonians, showing that half-gauging creates a non-trivial interface hosting scarred states protected by underlying symmetries.
AI.motivation: Quantum many-body scarring and symmetry defects are both active research areas, yet their interplay is poorly understood. The authors exploit a tractable class of models with zero-energy scarred states to explore how defect insertion, dualities, and half-gauging operations influence scarring, aiming to identify conditions for scar survival and to open directions for higher-dimensional scarred physics.
AI.method: The authors use a class of models derived from an embedding mechanism that defines a stochastic matrix form Hamiltonian hosting zero-energy many-body scarred states. They analyze the conditions under which scarred states persist after defect insertion, and perform a detailed analysis of half-gauging in such chains, which introduces a non-trivial interface in the system.
AI.result: The paper establishes the conditions required to retain scarred states after defect insertion within this model class. The central result is that half-gauging produces a non-trivial interface that hosts scarred states protected by the underlying symmetries.
AI.conclusion: The findings on half-gauged scarred systems are general and suggest promising directions for studying scarred physics in higher dimensions and assessing the robustness of scarred states.

title: Determination of Burgers-vector directions of threading edge dislocations in GaN by phase-contrast microscopy
summary: Phase-contrast microscopy enables rapid, nondestructive observation of threading dislocations in GaN, but the relationship between dislocation contrast and the Burgers vector has not been established. Here, we demonstrate that the in-plane Burgers-vector direction of threading edge dislocations in GaN can be determined from the arrangement of bright and dark contrast in phase-contrast microscopy images. The relationship was first established for threading edge dislocations in ammonothermal GaN whose Burgers vectors were independently determined by X-ray topography and was subsequently applied to hydride vapor phase epitaxy-grown GaN. The Burgers vector predicted from the phase contrast was verified by weak-beam dark-field TEM and large-angle convergent-beam electron diffraction. For the threading edge dislocations examined, the direction obtained by rotating the direction from the minimum of the dark contrast to the maximum of the bright contrast by 90° counterclockwise coincided with the Burgers-vector direction. Analysis based on the photoelastic effect further suggests that the phase contrast primarily reflects the sum of the two in-plane normal strain components, εxx + εyy, around the dislocation. These results demonstrate that phase-contrast microscopy can be used as a nondestructive optical method for determining the in-plane Burgers-vector direction of threading edge dislocations in GaN.

AI.tldr: Phase-contrast microscopy contrast in GaN can determine the in-plane Burgers-vector direction of threading edge dislocations, as the direction rotated 90° counterclockwise from dark minimum to bright maximum coincides with the Burgers vector.
AI.motivation: Phase-contrast microscopy allows rapid, nondestructive observation of threading dislocations in GaN, but the relationship between dislocation contrast and the Burgers vector had not been established, limiting its utility for defect characterization.
AI.method: The contrast–Burgers-vector relationship was first established for threading edge dislocations in ammonothermal GaN whose Burgers vectors were independently determined by X-ray topography, then applied to hydride vapor phase epitaxy-grown GaN. Predictions from phase contrast were verified by weak-beam dark-field TEM and large-angle convergent-beam electron diffraction. Photoelastic-effect analysis was used to interpret the contrast origin.
AI.result: For the examined threading edge dislocations, rotating the direction from the dark-contrast minimum to the bright-contrast maximum by 90° counterclockwise coincided with the in-plane Burgers-vector direction. Photoelastic analysis suggests the phase contrast primarily reflects the sum of the two in-plane normal strain components, εxx + εyy, around the dislocation.
AI.conclusion: Phase-contrast microscopy is established as a nondestructive optical method for determining the in-plane Burgers-vector direction of threading edge dislocations in GaN.

title: Analytical results for the Shannon entropy of the critical transverse-field Ising chain
summary: Local-basis Shannon entropies of critical wave functions contain universal subleading information, but the Shannon point of the critical transverse-field Ising chain is singular in the conventional Rényi approach. We treat it directly at $n=1$ by representing the complete computational-basis Born distribution as the odd-degree boundary of independent long-range Bernoulli edges. The Shannon chain rule separates the entropy into explicit independent-edge and conditional cycle-space terms. title: Layered spin-crossover metal-organic frameworks for light-induced control of two-dimensional quantum materials
summary: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are widely explored for gas separation, catalysis or energy storage, yet their integration with other electronically functional materials remains largely unexplored. Here, we integrate the layered Hofmann-type spin-crossover (SCO) MOF {FeII(pyS2Et)2[PtII(CN)4]} into electrical nanodevices to control the properties of two-dimensional (2D) quantum materials. In graphene, the conductivity is selectively switched by light. In spin-valves based on CrSBr bilayers, the MOF triggers magnetic hysteresis (absent in pristine CrSBr) and enables tunable non-volatile zero-field memory. In NbSe2, light modulates the superconducting critical current and transition temperature. These results establish layered stimuli-responsive SCO MOFs as active molecular control elements for 2D quantum materials, providing a route to strain-mediated control of electronic, magnetic, and superconducting functionalities and extending MOF-based architectures beyond traditional porous-matter applications towards multifunctional electronics and spintronics.

title: Interfacial Charge Transfer and Morphology Govern Magnetism in Ultrathin VOx/MoSe2 Heterostructures
summary: Engineering magnetism in two-dimensional semiconductors through interfacial interactions offers an attractive alternative to substitutional doping and provides opportunities for integrating magnetic and optoelectronic functionality within the same heterostructure. Here, we investigate ultrathin VOx films deposited on monolayer MoSe2 and demonstrate a pronounced enhancement of the magnetic response upon formation of the VOx/MoSe2 interface. Combined structural, spectroscopic, magnetic, and first-principles analyses support a consistent picture in which finite VOx clusters possess intrinsic magnetic moments that are further enhanced by electron transfer from MoSe2 to the oxide. The predicted charge transfer is also consistent with the increased trion contribution observed in the photoluminescence response of the heterostructure. Beyond this interfacial enhancement, the magnetic behavior is strongly governed by the morphology of the ultrathin oxide. A crossover from discontinuous clusters to more continuous films produces qualitatively different temperature dependences: the continuous-film regime exhibits conventional thermal demagnetization and coercive softening, whereas the clustered regime displays an unusual increase in magnetization and nonmonotonic coercivity with increasing temperature. These contrasting responses are captured by a phenomenological model in which morphology determines the collective magnetic dynamics through a distribution of effective reversal barriers and their thermally activated accessibility. Together, the results establish a unified picture in which interfacial charge transfer enhances the local magnetic moments of VOx, while nanoscale morphology governs their collective magnetic dynamics, providing complementary routes for controlling magnetism in oxide/transition-metal dichalcogenide heterostructures.

title: Exchange self-energy and vertex corrections to static screening in the two-dimensional electron gas
summary: We compute analytically the leading beyond-ring corrections to the static irreducible polarizability of the two-dimensional (2D) electron gas, namely the two exchange self-energy diagrams and the exchange vertex diagram, each of first order in the Coulomb coupling, and insert the resulting polarizability into the RPA geometric series to obtain the static dielectric function and screened interaction. The self-energy and vertex contributions individually diverge; we obtain both divergent pieces in closed form. Their sum is finite and reproduces exactly the Hartree-Fock compressibility, which renormalizes the Thomas-Fermi wave vector. We show that exchange converts the one-sided 2D Kohn kink at 2k_F into a sharp two-sided peak, a qualitative improvement over Thomas-Fermi and RPA screening. In real space this makes the Friedel oscillations around a charged impurity 2-3 times larger than in RPA, with an amplitude that increases with distance over the range studied; implications for Kohn-Luttinger pairing are discussed. Relation to earlier works on the same diagrams is discussed.

title: A self-learning scientific agent for X-ray diffraction
summary: A central challenge for scientific agents is to turn analytical experience into reusable expertise grounded in physical evidence. Here we introduce Gan Jiang, a self-learning agent for powder X-ray diffraction built on a diffraction-analysis ecosystem we developed: XMatcher, XQueryer, XDecomposer and WPEM. Together, these engines span phase identification, multiphase decomposition and physics-constrained whole-pattern modelling. Gan Jiang converts analytical experience into executable skills by diagnosing failures, revising skill instructions and code, and validating revisions before reuse, without retraining the language model or changing the underlying physical models. Skills selected using development data and frozen before held-out evaluation achieve higher refinement scores than the original expert-designed skills across FullProf, GSAS-II and PyWPEM. The agent resolves strongly overlapping reflections, quantifies a five-phase ancient Egyptian cosmetic, tracks lattice evolution in an operating battery and compares atomic configurations in a disordered oxide catalyst. On DeltaXRDbench, it leads the evaluated methods in single- and multiphase identification across simulated and experimental data. Without supplied composition, single-phase top-1 accuracies reach 96.30\%, 81.78\% and 40.83\% on MP500, RRUFF and opXRD, respectively, compared with 58.00\%, 58.47\% and 26.45\% for the strongest comparator.
